title: My Flutter App Was Buttery at 20 Widgets. At 2,000 It Dropped to 31 FPS.
excerpt: Ten mistakes that were quietly murdering my frame rate, and the exact fixes that got me back to a locked 60. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Flutter Flutter App Development UI Design Programming Android My Flutter App Was Buttery at 20 Widgets. At 2,000 It Dropped to 31 FPS. Mrityunjay Patel 7 min read · Jul 11, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Ten mistakes that were quietly murdering my frame rate, and the exact fixes that got me back to a locked 60. During development everything felt great. Twenty mock items scrolled like glass. I shipped the screen, connected the real API, and watched two thousand cards pour in with network images and a live “time ago” label ticking away. The list started to stutter. I turned on the performance overlay and there it was, a wall of red bars and a number I couldn’t unsee: 31 fps. Nothing was “wrong.” No crash, no error, no red screen. The app was just slow in that soft, embarrassing way that makes people quietly uninstall. So I spent a weekend profiling it, and almost every problem came down to the same ten mistakes. Here they are, with the code that caused them and the code that fixed them. First, the only number that matters: 16 milliseconds Flutter tries to render at 60 frames per second, and at 120 fps on displays that support it. At 60 fps, the framework has roughly 16.6 milliseconds to build, lay out, and paint every single frame. At 120 fps that budget shrinks to about 8 milliseconds. That number is the whole game. Every mistake below is really just one thing: something is stealing milliseconds you don’t have. Blow the budget and Flutter drops the frame, and the human holding the phone feels it as jank. Press enter or click to view image in full size The whole job in one picture: fit build, layout, and paint inside ~16.6 ms, or the frame drops. Mistake 1: Forgetting const constructors This was my most common sin. Every time a widget rebuilds, Flutter recreates all the child widget objects it returns, even the ones that never change. A const widget is created once at compile time and reused forever, so Flutter can skip rebuilding it entirely. In a long list, that is the difference between smooth and stuttering. // Bad: rebuilt on every parent rebuild return Padding( padding: EdgeInsets.all(16), child: Text('Comments'), ); // Good: created once, reused forever return const Padding( padding: EdgeInsets.all(16), child: Text('Comments'), ); Mistake 2: Building whole lists with ListView instead of ListView.builder A plain ListView with a children list builds every item up front, even the 1,980 the user will never scroll to. This was a big chunk of my 31 fps. ListView.builder is lazy: it only builds items as they scroll into view, so a list of 20 and a list of 20,000 cost roughly the same on first paint. // Bad: builds all 2,000 rows immediately ListView( children: items.map((i) => ProductCard(i)).toList(), ); // Good: builds only what's on screen ListView.builder( itemCount: items.length, itemBuilder: (context, i) => ProductCard(items[i]), ); Mistake 3: Reaching for shrinkWrap: true to silence an error Nest a ListView inside a Column and you get an unbounded-height error. The tempting one-line fix is shrinkWrap: true. It works, but it is a trap: shrinkWrap forces the scroll view to measure all of its children just to compute its own height, which throws away the lazy building you wanted. Nine times out of ten the real answer is a CustomScrollView with slivers, or giving the list a bounded height with Expanded. // Bad: measures every child up front ListView(shrinkWrap: true, children: rows); // Good: let a sliver handle it lazily CustomScrollView( slivers: [ SliverList.builder( itemCount: rows.length, itemBuilder: (_, i) => rows[i], ), ], ); Mistake 4: Calling setState() too high in the tree My live “time ago” label sat near the top of the screen, and I called setState() on the whole page to update it every second. That rebuilt the entire subtree, including the 2,000-item list, once a second. setState() rebuilds the widget it is called in and everything below it. The fix is to push the rebuild down: extract the changing part into its own small StatefulWidget so only that leaf rebuilds while the rest of the tree stays untouched. // Bad: setState here rebuilds the list too setState(() => _label = timeAgo(post.date)); // Good: only the clock widget rebuilds class TimeAgoLabel extends StatefulWidget { ... } // ...inside its own State: setState(() => _label = timeAgo(widget.date)); Press enter or click to view image in full size Same update, two blast radii. Move setState() to the leaf and the list stops rebuilding. Mistake 5: Animating with the Opacity widget To fade my cards in, I wrapped them in an Opacity widget and animated the value myself. Opacity is one of the more expensive widgets: at fractional values it forces Flutter to allocate an offscreen buffer with saveLayer and composite through it, every single frame of the animation. AnimatedOpacity and FadeTransition are built for exactly this, and the framework only pays that offscreen cost while the animation is actually running. // Bad: rebuilds + offscreen buffer every frame Opacity(opacity: _value, child: card); // Good: framework-optimized fade AnimatedOpacity( opacity: _visible ? 1 : 0, duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300), child: card, ); Mistake 6: Doing heavy work inside build() build() can be called 60 to 120 times a second, so it has to be cheap. I was sorting and formatting a list inside build(), which meant redoing that work on every frame. Anything that takes more than a fraction of a millisecond does not belong there. Move the expensive computation out, do it once in initState() or a controller, and let build() just read the cached result. // Bad: re-sorts on every single build Widget build(BuildContext context) { final sorted = items.toList()..sort(); return ItemList(sorted); } // Good: sort once, build just reads it late final List<Item> _sorted = items.toList()..sort(); Mistake 7: Parsing big JSON on the main thread The 2,000 cards arrived as one big JSON blob, and I called jsonDecode on it right in the widget. jsonDecode is s

title: Column-Level Encryption / Decryption with Oracle `DBMS_CRYPTO` in Spring Boot
excerpt: The problem Continue reading on Medium »
content: Spring Boot Oracle Crypto Kotlin Column-Level Encryption / Decryption with Oracle `DBMS_CRYPTO` in Spring Boot Anil Senocak 8 min read · Jul 11, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Column-Level Encryption / Decryption with Oracle `DBMS_CRYPTO` in Spring Boot The problem Most “the database is encrypted” stories stop at Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) the datafiles, redo logs, and backups are encrypted on disk, so an attacker who steals the raw .dbf files or a tape backup gets ciphertext. That's necessary but not sufficient. Once anyone, a DBA, an analyst with read-only access, an attacker who phished a service account, an unauthorized tool that landed a SELECT * query opens a connection to the database, TDE has already decrypted everything for them. The whole "encryption" boundary lives at the storage layer, not at the column. For regulated data (national-ID numbers, phone numbers, addresses under KVKK/GDPR; cardholder data under PCI-DSS; PHI under HIPAA), this gap matters: a leak through a legitimate DB connection is the most common breach path, not raw disk theft. The mitigation is column-level encryption the bytes physically stored in the firstname / lastname columns are ciphertext, and decryption only happens when the right key is presented. A DBA running SELECT firstname FROM users sees HEXTORAW('A8C1...') , not Anıl . GitHub - senocak/Spring-Oracle-Column-Level-Encryption-Decryption: Spring Oracle Column Level… Spring Oracle Column Level Encryption Decryption. Contribute to… github.com The naive way to do this is to encrypt in the application call a crypto.encrypt(...) helper before every repository.save() and a crypto.decrypt(...) after every findBy*() . This works for trivial CRUD but falls apart fast: Every query path has to remember. Native queries, reporting jobs, batch importers, JdbcTemplate one-offs, raw EntityManager.createQuery calls each one is an opportunity to forget the wrapper and either store plaintext or read ciphertext as garbage. WHERE / LIKE / ORDER BY break. The database can only compare what it can see. If the column is ciphertext, a LIKE '%anıl%' predicate matches nothing — you either have to pull every row to the app and filter in memory, or build an awkward "encrypt the search term and compare ciphertext" path that only works for exact equality with a deterministic cipher. Migrations and ad-hoc fixes hurt. Anyone running a Flyway script or a one-off UPDATE has to know the encryption convention and apply it manually. The leak surface is wide. Every Kotlin call site, every test fixture, every seed data loader has to be reviewed. Miss one, and that column ends up half-encrypted forever. The Solution What this project solves: the encryption boundary is pushed down into the database into a pair of SQL functions ( encrypt_text / decrypt_text ) that are the only point at which plaintext and ciphertext meet. Hibernate's @ColumnTransformer then makes the application physically unable to bypass them: every query Hibernate generates including JPA Criteria predicates used for LIKE filtering is rewritten at the ORM level to call those functions. Application code reads and writes Kotlin String values exactly as if the column were unencrypted; WHERE firstname LIKE '%anıl%' works against the decrypted value because the SQL Hibernate sends is WHERE LOWER(decrypt_text(firstname)) LIKE ? . Backups, exports, replicas, and SELECT * from a DBA's IDE all see ciphertext. The only way to read plaintext is to be a session that holds the key, and the key never appears in application code at all. This project shows how to push column-level encryption into the database while keeping the application code free of any awareness of it. The Spring/Kotlin/JPA layer reads and writes plain Kotlin String values; ciphertext lives only inside the database column, and the encryption/decryption hop happens inside a pair of SQL functions that the database invokes on every read and write. The entity declares an encrypt_text(text) / decrypt_text(raw) function pair and wires them into the column via @ColumnTransformer . Hibernate then rewrites every generated query to call those functions automatically. Core idea Hibernate’s @ColumnTransformer lets you inject a SQL expression around a column on read and on write. Anywhere Hibernate would emit SELECT firstname FROM users it instead emits SELECT decrypt_text(firstname) FROM users , and anywhere it would emit INSERT ... VALUES (?) it emits INSERT ... VALUES (encrypt_text(?)) . Critically, this applies to every Hibernate-generated query - including JPA Criteria queries used for filtering - so a LIKE '%anıl%' on firstname becomes a LIKE on the decrypted value, transparently. The entity declaration is the whole contract: @Entity @Table(name = "users") class User( @Column(name = "firstname", nullable = false, columnDefinition = "RAW(2000)") @ColumnTransformer( read  = "decrypt_text(firstname)", write = "encrypt_text(?)" ) var firstname: String, @Column(name = "lastname", nullable = false, columnDefinition = "RAW(2000)") @ColumnTransformer( read  = "decrypt_text(lastname)", write = "encrypt_text(?)" ) var lastname: String ) : BaseDomain() From this point on, the rest of the application ( UserRepository , the /users controller, the JPA Specification that builds LIKE predicates) is written as if firstname and lastname were ordinary VARCHAR columns. How a request flows end-to-end GET /users?firstname=Anıl3&lastname=Senocak3 triggers the following: Controller builds a JPA Specification containing two LIKE predicates against root.get("firstname") and root.get("lastname") . Hibernate plans the query. Because of @ColumnTransformer(read = ...) , the projected columns and the predicate columns are rewritten to wrap the raw column in decrypt_text(...) . title: Mastering Ktor: End-to-End Guide for Android, KMP & Backend Development
excerpt: How to build a shared networking layer with Ktor Client, power it with a Ktor Server backend, and consume it from Mobile apps all without… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Multiplatform Ktor Jetpack Compose Backend Development Mastering Ktor: End-to-End Guide for Android, KMP & Backend Development Kaushal Vasava 12 min read · Jul 22, 2026 -- Listen Share How to build a shared networking layer with Ktor Client, power it with a Ktor Server backend, and consume it from Mobile apps all without leaving Kotlin. Press enter or click to view image in full size If you’ve spent any time in the Kotlin ecosystem, you’ve probably noticed a quiet shift: the line between “backend developer” and “Android developer” is disappearing. A big reason for that is Ktor — JetBrains’ asynchronous framework that works as both an HTTP server and an HTTP client , and runs on the JVM, Android, iOS (via Kotlin/Native), and even the browser. That means you can write your REST API in Ktor Server, write the code that calls that API in Ktor Client, share the client code across Android and iOS through Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP), and never switch languages once. This guide covers all three pieces, with a deep, hands-on focus on the part most people actually spend their time writing: Ktor Client — its HTTP methods, request/response handling, and plugins. We’ll build a small but complete Task Manager system: A Ktor Server backend exposing a REST API A shared KMP module with a Ktor Client that talks to that API An Android app (Jetpack Compose) that consumes the shared module A look at how the same shared code plugs into iOS Versions used in this article (check for newer patch releases before you start): Kotlin 2.4.x, Ktor 3.5.x, Gradle 8.x, JDK 17+. The core APIs shown here have been stable across Ktor 2.x and 3.x. What We’re Building ┌───────────────────────────┐ │        Ktor Server         │ │   (Netty engine, JVM)       │ │   REST API for Tasks        │ └──────────────┬─────────────┘ │ HTTP / JSON │ ┌──────────────▼─────────────────────────┐ │      Shared KMP Module (commonMain)      │ │   Ktor Client + kotlinx.serialization     │ └───────┬───────────────────────┬─────────┘ │                       │ ┌───────▼────────┐     ┌────────▼────────┐ │   Android App    │     │     iOS App      │ │ (OkHttp engine)   │     │ (Darwin engine)  │ └───────────────────┘     └──────────────────┘ Part 1 — The Backend: Ktor Server (Quick Setup) We’ll keep this part lean since the real focus of this article is the client — but you need something to call. Project Setup // build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.0" id("io.ktor.plugin") version "3.5.0" kotlin("plugin.serialization") version "2.4.0" } dependencies { implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-core") implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-netty") implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-content-negotiation") implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-json") implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-call-logging") implementation("ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:1.5.6") } The Application Module, Data, and Routes @Serializable data class Task(val id: Int, val title: String, val done: Boolean = false) fun main() { embeddedServer(Netty, port = 8080, host = "0.0.0.0", module = Application::module) .start(wait = true) } fun Application.module() { install(ContentNegotiation) { json() } install(CallLogging) val tasks = mutableListOf( Task(1, "Learn Ktor Client"), Task(2, "Build the shared KMP module"), Task(3, "Wire it into Compose") ) var nextId = tasks.size + 1 routing { route("/tasks") { get { call.respond(tasks) } get("{id}") { val id = call.parameters["id"]?.toIntOrNull() val task = tasks.find { it.id == id } if (task != null) call.respond(task) else call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound) } post { val body = call.receive<Map<String, String>>() val task = Task(nextId++, body["title"] ?: "Untitled") tasks.add(task) call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, task) } delete("{id}") { val id = call.parameters["id"]?.toIntOrNull() tasks.removeAll { it.id == id } call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent) } } } } Run it with ./gradlew run , verify with curl http://localhost:8080/tasks , and let's move to the part you're really here for. Part 2 — Ktor Client Deep Dive This is the part most Android and KMP developers actually live in day to day, so let’s go slow. Creating a Client Every Ktor Client starts the same way: pick an engine (or let Ktor pick one automatically based on your classpath), then install the plugins you need. val client = HttpClient(CIO) { expectSuccess = true // throw exceptions on 4xx/5xx instead of silently returning them install(ContentNegotiation) { json(Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; isLenient = true }) } install(Logging) { level = LogLevel.INFO } install(HttpTimeout) { requestTimeoutMillis = 10_000 } defaultRequest { url("https://api.example.com/") contentType(ContentType.Application.Json) } } In a Kotlin Multiplatform commonMain source set you'd usually skip naming the engine ( HttpClient(CIO) → just HttpClient() ), and let each platform's classpath resolve to whichever single engine dependency it has (OkHttp on Android, Darwin on iOS, CIO on the JVM). One HttpClient instance should generally be reused for the lifetime of your app/module — creating a new one per request throws away connection pooling. The HTTP Methods Ktor Client exposes a top-level suspend function for each HTTP verb. All of them return an HttpResponse (or, with content negotiation, you can call .body<T>() directly on the result). // GET val tasks: List<Task> = client.get("tasks").body() // POST - send a body val created: Task = client.post("tasks") { setBody(Task(id = 0, title = "New task")) }.body() // PUT - full replace val replaced: Task = client.put("tasks/1") { setBody(Task(id = 1, title = "Updated title", done = true)) }.body() // PATCH - partial update val patched: Task = client.patch("tasks/1/toggle").body() // DELETE client.delete("tasks/1") // HEAD - headers only, no body val headResponse: HttpResponse = client.head("tasks") println(headResponse.headers[HttpHeaders.ContentLength]) // OPTIONS - discover allowed methods val optionsResponse: HttpResponse

title: Building High-Performance Text Editors in Kotlin Multiplatform with Krope
excerpt: If you have ever tried building a text editor, an IDE, or a collaborative document tool, you quickly run into a fundamental wall: how do… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Multiplatform Data Structures Performance Kotlin Software Engineering Building High-Performance Text Editors in Kotlin Multiplatform with Krope numq 6 min read · Jul 24, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size If you have ever tried building a text editor, an IDE, or a collaborative document tool, you quickly run into a fundamental wall: how do you store the text? At first glance, a standard String seems fine. But Strings are immutable; changing a single character in a 1MB file requires allocating a brand new 1MB array. So, you move to StringBuilder . It’s mutable and fast for simple appends, but inserting or deleting text in the middle of a massive document still requires shifting hundreds of thousands of characters in memory — an O(N) operation that causes UI stuttering as your document grows. This is where the Rope data structure comes in. Today, I want to introduce Krope , a high-performance, memory-safe, and reactive Rope library built entirely in Kotlin Multiplatform. Whether you are targeting JVM, Android, iOS, or WASM, Krope provides the engine you need to build next-generation text editing tools. What is a Rope? Instead of storing text as a single massive, contiguous array of characters, a Rope stores text as a balanced binary tree (in Krope’s case, utilizing a Red-Black tree variant). The leaves of the tree contain short chunks of strings. When you insert text in the middle of a document, a Rope doesn’t copy the whole string. Instead, it splits a leaf node and inserts a new branch. This gives operations like insertion, deletion, and replacement a time complexity of O(log N). Furthermore, Krope implements structural sharing . When a modification occurs, Krope doesn’t mutate the existing tree; it returns a new tree that shares the untouched branches with the old one. This provides safe concurrent access, cheap undo/redo history. Why I Built Krope The idea for Krope was born while building haskcore — a full-featured IDE for Haskell written in Compose Desktop. It uses Skia for rendering, Tree-sitter for incremental syntax parsing, and the Language Server Protocol for code intelligence. It’s a real editor with 40+ modules, handling everything from syntax highlighting to code completion and project-wide diagnostics. Very quickly, I hit a wall: Kotlin’s standard StringBuilder couldn't keep up. Editing large Haskell modules meant shifting massive text buffers on every keystroke, causing visible lag during syntax highlighting and LSP synchronization. I needed something better — and the rope data structure, battle-tested in editors like Emacs and Vim since the 90s, was the obvious answer. But Kotlin Multiplatform lacked a modern, reactive, and fully-featured rope implementation. So I built Krope to solve the specific pain points I encountered: Cross-Platform Consistency: haskcore targets the desktop, but the same text engine should work on Android, iOS, and WASM for future ports or companion apps. Reactive by Design: Compose Multiplatform thrives on reactive state. Krope exposes every edit as a SharedFlow event and every document state as a StateFlow , making UI integration seamless. Byte-Level Encoding Awareness: LSP servers speak in byte offsets, not character positions. Krope natively tracks UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32, giving you efficient access to byte coordinates backed by an LRU cache. Functional & Safe: Invalid operations shouldn’t crash your editor. Krope uses an Either<Throwable, Result> pattern, so out-of-bounds inserts return errors you can handle gracefully — critical when processing remote edits from LSP or collaborative peers. Inside the Krope API Krope separates the underlying data structure from the editor API. The primary interface you interact with is the TextBuffer . Here is how simple it is to get started: import io.github.numq.krope.core.Encoding import io.github.numq.krope.text.* import kotlinx.coroutines.launch // 1. Initialize the buffer val factory = RopeTextBufferFactory() val buffer = factory.create( text = "Hello World", encoding = Encoding.UTF8, lineEnding = TextLineEnding.LF, enablePooling = true // Enables internal string interning to save memory ).fold( onLeft = { error -> throw error }, onRight = { it } ) The Reactive Paradigm In a standard text editor, the UI needs to know exactly what changed to update the screen or send a diff over the network for collaborative editing. excerpt: Every Android engineer has shipped this without thinking twice about it. Continue reading on Stackademic »
content: Rust: Every try-catch You’ve Ever Written Was a Promise You Could Break, Result Isn’t Taufik Hidayat 7 min read · Jul 26, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Exception: One hides the failure. The other forces you to face it. Every Android engineer has shipped this without thinking twice about it. fun getUser(id: String): User { val response = api.fetchUser(id) // might throw return response.toUser() } fun main() { val user = getUser("123") // compiles fine, crashes at runtime println(user.name) } This compiles. Ship it, and somewhere in production, fetchUser throws an IOException nobody catches, and the app dies. The compiler never warned you. It never had to. throws in Kotlin is a suggestion, not a rule. fn get_user(id: &str) -> Result<User, ApiError> { let response = api::fetch_user(id)?; // might fail Ok(response.to_user()) } fn main() { let user = get_user("123"); // Result<User, ApiError>, not User println!("{}", user.unwrap().name); // compiler forces you to unwrap it first } This also compiles, but only because main was forced to acknowledge that get_user might fail. You can't print user.name directly. user isn't a User , it's a Result<User, ApiError> , a value that is either Ok(User) or Err(ApiError) , and the compiler will not let you touch what's inside until you say which one you're dealing with. In Part 6 , we talked about how Option<T> kills null at compile time. Turns out that's just half the story. Rust applies the exact same trick to something bigger: the entire concept of "this operation might fail." No exceptions, no try , no catch . Just a return type that tells the truth. A Type That Tells the Truth Rust has no exception mechanism. There’s no throw , no try-catch , no stack unwinding for normal error flow. Every function that can fail says so in its signature, Result<T, E> , and the caller can't touch what's inside without opening it first, through match , ? , or an explicit .unwrap() . The Developer This Changes First Android engineers who’ve written try { } catch (e: Exception) { } more times than they'd like to admit. Especially the ones who've caught a generic Exception , logged it, and moved on without really knowing what just happened or whether the app is still in a valid state. Where the Compiler Goes Quiet The moment this becomes personal is the moment an app crashes in production from an exception nobody planned for. Maybe it was an unchecked exception the type system never asked you to handle. Maybe it was a checked one you caught, logged, and silently swallowed, letting the app limp forward in a broken state instead of failing loudly. Either way, the compiler said nothing. It couldn’t. Kotlin’s checked exceptions are a JVM-level convention, not something the Kotlin compiler enforces the way it enforces null-safety. Rust doesn’t give you that option. If get_user can fail, Result<User, ApiError> is baked into its signature, and every caller has to open that box before touching what's inside. Three Levels In Level 1: Result<T, E> , the two-branch box enum Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E), } That’s it. That’s the whole mechanism. Result is an enum with exactly two variants, Ok holding a success value, Err holding an error value. No inheritance hierarchy, no checked-vs-unchecked distinction, no Throwable supertype. Just two boxes, and the compiler needs you to open the right one. fn divide(a: f64, b: f64) -> Result<f64, String> { if b == 0.0 { return Err("cannot divide by zero".to_string()); } Ok(a / b) } fn main() { match divide(10.0, 2.0) { Ok(result) => println!("Result:{}", result), Err(e) => println!("Error:{}", e), } } Same exhaustive match from Part 6. Miss the Err arm, the code doesn't compile. There's no code path where a failed division silently becomes a NaN or a crash three functions downstream. The failure is visible at the exact point where it happened. Level 2: ? , propagation without the boilerplate Matching every single Result gets old fast, especially when a function just wants to pass the error up the chain instead of handling it locally. That's what ? is for. fn get_user_email(id: &str) -> Result<String, ApiError> { let response = api::fetch_user(id)?; let user = response.to_user()?; Ok(user.email) } Each ? says: if this is Ok(value) , unwrap it and keep going. If it's Err(e) , stop right here and return that Err from the whole function. No catch , no throw , no exception bubbling up through five stack frames you didn't write and don't control. The function signature already told you get_user_email returns Result<String, ApiError> , so ? is just doing what the type already promised. Compare that to Kotlin. There’s no language-level equivalent. The closest is manually checking and re-throwing, or reaching for a Result -like wrapper class (Kotlin does have a kotlin.Result , but it's opt-in, and most codebases still lean on exceptions underneath it). Level 3: custom error types and combinators Real apps don’t fail with one error shape. A network call and a JSON parse fail differently, and lumping them into String errors (like the divide example) throws away information. This is where enum from Part 6 comes back. enum ApiError { Network(String), Parse(String), NotFound, } fn fetch_user(id: &str) -> Result<Response, ApiError> { let response = http_get(id).map_err(|e| ApiError::Network(e.to_string()))?; if response.status == 404 { return Err(ApiError::NotFound); } Ok(response) } ApiError is an exhaustive, closed set of everything that can go wrong in this domain. match on it later, and the compiler will remind you if a new variant shows up and you forgot to handle it. Try doing that with a Kotlin exception hierarchy and an open class you don't control. excerpt: Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. Every user has a name, email, and phone number. However, customers have shipping… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Inheritance in Kotlin: A Complete Guide to Reusing Code Effectively Tech Dynasty 5 min read · Jul 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. Every user has a name, email, and phone number. However, customers have shipping addresses, sellers have store information, and administrators have special permissions. Although these users have different responsibilities, they all share some common characteristics. Press enter or click to view image in full size Instead of rewriting the same properties and functions for every type of user, Kotlin allows us to reuse existing code through inheritance . Inheritance is one of the four fundamental principles of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). It helps developers create cleaner, reusable, and more maintainable applications by allowing one class to inherit the properties and behavior of another. In this article, you’ll learn how inheritance works in Kotlin, why classes are final by default, how to override members, and when inheritance should (and shouldn't) be used. What Is Inheritance? Inheritance is the mechanism by which one class acquires the properties and functions of another class. The class being inherited is called the: Parent Class Base Class Superclass The class that inherits from it is called the: Child Class Derived Class Subclass For example: Vehicle │ ┌───────┴────────┐ │                │ Car            Motorcycle Both Car and Motorcycle inherit common behavior from Vehicle . Why Use Inheritance? Without inheritance, you might end up writing the same code repeatedly. For example: class Customer { val name = "" val email = "" } class Seller { val name = "" val email = "" } Notice that both classes duplicate the same properties. Instead, move the shared functionality into a parent class. open class User( val name: String, val email: String ) Now both Customer and Seller can inherit from User . This reduces duplication and keeps the code easier to maintain. Classes Are final by Default One important difference between Kotlin and Java is that every class is final by default . class Animal This class cannot be inherited. If you try: class Dog : Animal() The compiler reports an error. Why? Because Kotlin encourages composition over inheritance and prevents accidental extension of classes. Making a Class Inheritable with open To allow inheritance, mark the parent class with the open keyword. open class Animal Now another class can inherit from it. class Dog : Animal() Here: Animal is the parent class. Dog is the child class. Inheriting Properties Parent class: open class Person( val name: String, val age: Int ) Child class: class Student( name: String, age: Int, val grade: String ) : Person(name, age) Usage: val student = Student( "Janhvi", 24, "A" ) println(student.name) println(student.grade) Output: Janhvi A The child class automatically gets access to the parent’s properties. Inheriting Functions Functions are also inherited. open class Animal { fun eat() { println("Eating...") } } Child class: class Dog : Animal() Usage: val dog = Dog() dog.eat() Output: Eating... Even though Dog doesn't define eat() , it inherits it from Animal . Overriding Functions Sometimes the inherited implementation isn’t suitable. For example, every animal makes a different sound. Parent class: open class Animal { open fun makeSound() { println("Animal Sound") } } Notice the open keyword. Now the child class can provide its own implementation. class Dog : Animal() { override fun makeSound() { println("Bark") } } Usage: val dog = Dog() dog.makeSound() Output: Bark Overriding Properties Properties can also be overridden. Parent: open class Employee { open val role = "Employee" } Child: class Manager : Employee() { override val role = "Manager" } Usage: println(Manager().role) Output: Manager Calling the Parent Implementation with super Sometimes you want to extend the parent’s behavior instead of replacing it completely. open class Animal { open fun makeSound() { println("Animal Sound") } } Child class: class Dog : Animal() { override fun makeSound() { super.makeSound() println("Bark") } } Output: Animal Sound Bark The super keyword calls the implementation from the parent class. Constructor in Inheritance When a child class inherits from a parent, it must initialize the parent first. open class User( val name: String ) class Customer( name: String ) : User(name) The parent constructor runs before the child constructor. Multi-Level Inheritance Inheritance can continue across multiple levels. Vehicle │ Car │ ElectricCar Example: open class Vehicle open class Car : Vehicle() class ElectricCar : Car() Although possible, deep inheritance hierarchies should be avoided because they make code harder to understand. Real-World Android Examples Base Activity Many Android projects create a common base activity. open class BaseActivity { fun showLoading() { println("Loading...") } } Every screen can inherit common functionality. class HomeActivity : BaseActivity() class LoginActivity : BaseActivity() User Models open class User( val id: Int, val name: String ) class Customer( id: Int, name: String, val address: String ) : User(id, name) class Seller( id: Int, name: String, val storeName: String ) : User(id, name) This avoids duplicating common user information. Payment Methods open class Payment { open fun pay() { println("Processing payment") } } class CardPayment : Payment() { override fun pay() { println("Paid using Card") } } class UpiPayment : Payment() { override fun pay() { println("Paid using UPI") } } Different payment methods share the same interface but provide different implementations. Inheritance vs Composition A common guideline in Kotlin is: Prefer composition over inheritance. Instead of inheriting just to reuse code, consider whether one class should simply contain another. What is Composition? Composition means building one class using another class . It

content: Kotlin Android Development Kotlin Coroutines Programming Software Engineering Your First Kotlin Coroutine: A Beginner’s Guide to suspend, launch, and async Mahmoud Ramadan 10 min read · Jul 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Read More https://leanpub.com/master_coroutine_flow In Chapter 1, suspend was a promise. In this chapter, we cash it in: what a suspending function really is, how to run one, and what "suspension" looks like once you stop trusting the magic. 2.1 The suspend Keyword A suspending function is an ordinary function with one extra ability: it can pause and resume without blocking the thread it runs on. You mark it with the suspend modifier: suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): User { delay(1000)               // pause for 1s, without blocking the thread return User(id, "Mahmoud") } delay is the coroutine world's equivalent of Thread.sleep , with one all-important difference. Thread.sleep(1000) blocks — the thread sits there doing nothing for a full second. delay(1000) suspends — the coroutine steps aside for a second and the thread is released to do other work . After a second, the coroutine resumes on the next line. Same observable delay, completely different cost. Here’s the rule that governs everything: a suspending function can only be called from another suspending function, or from inside a coroutine. It cannot be called from regular code. fun regularFunction() { fetchUser("1")  // ❌ compile error: suspend function called from non-suspend context } suspend fun anotherSuspendFunction() { fetchUser("1")  // ✅ fine — we're already in a suspend function } Why the restriction? Because suspension only works if the caller knows how to handle a pause. A regular function has no machinery for “pause here and come back later.” A suspend function does. So suspend is contagious in the upward direction — call a suspend function and your function must become suspend too, all the way up until you hit a coroutine builder , which is where a regular function finally bridges into the coroutine world. This raises the obvious question: if suspend functions can only be called by other suspend functions, how does the very first one get called? That’s what builders are for. 2.2 Bridging Into Coroutines: runBlocking To call a suspend function from regular code, you need to start a coroutine. The simplest builder for learning (and for tests, and for main functions) is runBlocking : fun main() { println("Before") runBlocking { val user = fetchUser("1")   // ✅ we're inside a coroutine now println("Got: ${user.name}") } println("After") } Output: Before Got: Mahmoud After runBlocking does exactly what its name says: it blocks the current thread until the coroutine inside it completes. It is a bridge between the blocking world (regular functions, main , JUnit tests) and the suspending world (everything inside the lambda). That blocking behavior is also why you almost never use runBlocking in production Android code. Blocking is the very thing we're trying to escape — using runBlocking on the main thread reintroduces the freeze from Chapter 1. Its legitimate homes are: The main() function of a command-line program. Unit tests (though we’ll prefer runTest later — see Chapter 18). Occasionally, bridging into a legacy blocking API at the edge of your system. Inside an Android app, you’ll start coroutines with launch and async instead, tied to a proper scope. Let's meet those. 2.3 The Two Workhorses: launch and async To start a coroutine that does not block the caller, you use launch or async . Both are extension functions on CoroutineScope (we'll formally define scope in Chapter 4; for now, think of it as "the context a coroutine lives in"). They differ in one way: what they give back. launch — fire and forget launch starts a coroutine and returns a Job , a handle you can use to cancel it or wait for it. It does not return a result. Use it for work whose side effects matter but whose return value you don't need — saving to a database, updating UI state, logging. fun loadData(scope: CoroutineScope) { scope.launch { val user = fetchUser("1") updateUi(user)          // side effect; no value handed back to caller } // this line runs immediately — launch did not block } async — I need a result back async starts a coroutine and returns a Deferred<T> , a promise of a future value. You call .await() on it (a suspending call) to get the result when it's ready. suspend fun loadData(scope: CoroutineScope) { val deferred: Deferred<User> = scope.async { fetchUser("1") } val user = deferred.await()   // suspends until the result is ready updateUi(user) } On its own, a single async immediately followed by await is just a more roundabout suspend call. Its real power shows up with parallelism , which is the next section. Rule of thumb: launch when you don't need a result; async when you do. Reaching for async and immediately await ing it on the next line is usually a sign you wanted a plain suspend call. 2.4 Running Work in Parallel Return to the profile loader. Suppose the user and their settings come from two independent endpoints — neither depends on the other. Written sequentially, we pay for both round-trips one after another: suspend fun loadProfile(): Profile { val user = fetchUser("1")        // 1 second val settings = fetchSettings("1") // 1 second return Profile(user, settings)    // total: ~2 seconds } Two seconds, even though the calls don’t depend on each other. We’re leaving time on the table. With async , we start both before awaiting either: suspend fun loadProfile(): Profile = coroutineScope { val userDeferred = async { fetchUser("1") }         // starts immediately val settingsDeferred = async { fetchSettings("1") } // starts immediately val user = userDeferred.await()       // both are already in flight val settings = settingsDeferred.await() Profile(user, settings)               // total: ~1 second } Both requests are now in flight at the same time, so the total

content: Kotlin Flutter Compose Multiplatform Android IOS Why I’m Learning Compose Multiplatform in 2026 Hilmy SF 3 min read · 6 days ago -- Listen Share The first thing that confused me about Jetpack Compose wasn’t the syntax — it was the mental model. In Flutter, you pass children as a parameter. In Compose, you define them inside a trailing lambda. That alone took some getting used to, but the bigger struggle came when I tried styling a simple custom shape with Box. In Flutter, Container comes with built-in parameters to customize its shape. In Compose, you have to chain Modifier functions to achieve the same thing, and at first, I often didn’t know which one to use. It took me far longer than it should have to recreate a shape I was already used to making instantly in Flutter. I’ve worked as a mobile app developer for 4 years, the first 2 of which were with Flutter. When I moved to a new company, I joined a project to revamp an existing Flutter app using Compose Multiplatform — that’s when I started learning Kotlin and Compose. So why did we choose Compose Multiplatform instead of sticking with Flutter? The first and main reason is that our team was already familiar with Kotlin. Our main product, an Android-native app, is built entirely with it. The other reason was more practical: Kotlin’s interoperability with Objective-C/Swift APIs meant we wouldn’t need to build a bridge for every native feature, the way Flutter relies on platform channels. I tried this myself with the camera — just getting a basic preview to show up — and being able to call the native API directly, without writing a platform channel, made the whole process feel much simpler. Coming from BLOC, I could barely read the code at first. For me, it involved too much boilerplate, and working with BlocBuilder, BlocListener, and BlocConsumer never quite clicked. With MVI in Compose, I don’t need those separate wrapper widgets — I can observe state and effects directly using collectAsState and LaunchedEffect. What helped even more was how Kotlin represents Event and State as sealed classes and data classes. Once that clicked, handling every possible state through a single onIntent/onEvent function finally made sense to me. Even so, I still have concerns about where CMP is headed. Compared to Flutter, its community is much smaller — more than once, I’ve run into errors with barely any discussion or documentation to help me work through them. Core functionality like navigation still relies on a third-party library, Voyager, instead of something official. I also still miss Flutter’s hot reload — it applies changes directly to the running app, so I could see the result instantly on a real device or emulator. Compose Preview lets me see the UI too, but only on a static canvas, not inside the app that’s actually running. I also haven’t worked with hardware integrations like Bluetooth or GPS yet, so I can’t speak to that experience. I’m still early in this journey, and I don’t think CMP is objectively better than Flutter — it’s just what made sense for my team’s context. If you’re exploring CMP yourself, or went through the same Flutter-to-Compose transition, I’d love to hear what your experience has been like.

Everything below explains how I got here and why each piece exists. yaml stages: - test - build - deploy # Runs validation checks for MRs and master test: stage: test image: mingc/android-build-box:latest rules: - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"' - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "master"' script: - ./gradlew test # Fast build check for feature branches / MRs # Does not create a release artifact build_check: stage: build image: mingc/android-build-box:latest rules: - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"' script: - ./gradlew assembleDebug # Production release build # Runs only after merging into master # Creates signed AAB and runs release build pipeline build_aab: stage: build image: mingc/android-build-box:latest rules: - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "master"' before_script: - ruby -v - gem install bundler - bundle install # Restore Android signing configuration - echo "$KEYSTORE_FILE_BASE64" | base64 -d > app/keystore/nhl-release.jks - echo "storeFile=keystore/nhl-release.jks" > keystore.properties - echo "storePassword=$KEYSTORE_STORE_PASSWORD" >> keystore.properties - echo "keyAlias=$KEYSTORE_KEY_ALIAS" >> keystore.properties - echo "keyPassword=$KEYSTORE_KEY_PASSWORD" >> keystore.properties script: # Generates release AAB (R8 runs if enabled) - bundle exec fastlane run gradle task:"bundle" build_type:"Release" artifacts: # Pass AAB to deploy job paths: - app/build/outputs/bundle/release/*.aab expire_in: 1 week # Upload release artifact to Google Play # Only runs for master branch deploy_playstore: stage: deploy image: mingc/android-build-box:latest rules: - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "master"' # Wait for successful AAB build needs: - build_aab before_script: - ruby -v - gem install bundler - bundle install # Restore Android signing configuration - echo "$KEYSTORE_FILE_BASE64" | base64 -d > app/keystore/nhl-release.jks - echo "storeFile=keystore/nhl-release.jks" > keystore.properties - echo "storePassword=$KEYSTORE_STORE_PASSWORD" >> keystore.properties - echo "keyAlias=$KEYSTORE_KEY_ALIAS" >> keystore.properties - echo "keyPassword=$KEYSTORE_KEY_PASSWORD" >> keystore.properties # Google Play API credentials - cp "$GOOGLE_PLAY_JSON_KEY" fastlane/google-play-key.json script: # Uploads AAB to Google Play - bundle exec fastlane playstore The flow it produces: (ticket124 branch) | |  push commits v Open MR → dev | v GitLab MR Pipeline | +--> test (./gradlew test) | +--> build_check (assembleDebug) | v Review / Approve | v Merge → dev | v (no deploy happens) ------------------------------- (dev or release branch) | | create release OR MR → master v Open MR → master | v GitLab MR Pipeline | +--> test (./gradlew test) | +--> build_check (assembleDebug) | v Review / Approve | v Merge → master | v GitLab MASTER Pipeline | +--> test (run again on final code) | +--> build_aab (bundleRelease + R8) | +--> deploy_playstore | v 🚀 Google Play Upload Okay. Now let’s talk about how I actually got here, because it was not a straight line. 😅 🎬 Part 1: “Wait, How Do I Actually Deploy?” Lacking any release pipeline, I used to simply execute commands from my terminal locally to push builds to app stores, meaning my first instinct was running bundle exec fastlane supply directly — the raw fastlane action for publishing to Google Play. It failed instantly: 😭 [!] No local metadata, apks, aab, or track to promote were found Why: fastlane supply only uploads — it has zero knowledge of Gradle or how to build your app. It's not a build tool. The fix was checking the project’s actual Fastfile , which already had a lane for exactly this: ruby desc "Deploy a new version to the Google Play Store (using AAB)" lane :playstore do gradle(task: 'bundle', build_type: 'Release') upload_to_play_store( skip_upload_apk: true, track: "production", ) end So the actual command was just: bash bundle exec fastlane playstore This builds and uploads in one shot. 🎉 (Tip: run bundle exec fastlane lanes any time you forget what lanes exist in a project.) 🔓 Part 2: The Security Detour (Important!) While reading app/build.gradle.kts to understand the signing setup, this showed up: kotlin signingConfigs { create("release") { keyAlias = "blah" keyPassword = "blah" storeFile = file("../app/keystore/blah-release.jks") storePassword = "blah" } } 😬 The actual keystore file and its passwords, hardcoded in plaintext, committed to git. This matters because: Anyone with repo access can pull the signing key straight out of git history A leaked signing key can be used to publish malicious updates to your live app under your identity It’s permanently in every commit that touched this file unless you rewrite history How bad was it, really? Two things saved me from a genuine emergency: Private repo — not zero risk, but way lower than public exposure Play App Signing was enabled ( Play Console → Setup → App signing showed "Releases signed by Play ✅"). This means Google holds the real signing key — what was in the repo was only an upload key . If that leaks, you request an upload-key reset through Play Console. No app disruption, no drama. ⚠️ If you’re not on Play App Signing and your real release key leaks, it’s a much bigger deal — that key must sign every future update forever, and recovering from a leak requires contacting Google support for a manual key-upgrade process. Check your own setup: Play Console → your app → Setup → App signing . title: We Built an Offline Scam Checker for India. Here Is Why.
excerpt: Seerie is live on Google Play. It checks scams on your phone, works without internet, and never sends your messages to a server. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Cybersecurity India Privacy Fraud Prevention Android Seerror 4 min read · Jul 25, 2026 -- Listen Share We Built an Offline Scam Checker for India. Here Is Why. Seerie is live on Google Play. It checks scams on your phone, works without internet, and never sends your messages to a server. There is a window after a scam, sometimes as short as three minutes, where the money can still be stopped. Banks can freeze a transfer. A UPI collect request can be declined before it clears. A call can be cut before the next instruction lands. Almost nobody uses that window well. Not because people are careless, but because in those three minutes they do not know what to do first. Call the bank? Call 1930? Go to the police station? File on cybercrime.gov.in? The correct answer is several of those, in a specific order, and nobody tells you the order while your hands are shaking. That is the gap Seerie was built for. The problem is not awareness. It is the first step. Over eleven lakh cyber fraud complaints were filed in India last year. Thousands of crores lost. Most victims never recovered anything. We spoke to people who had been scammed, and the same three barriers came up every time. Language. Most portals and helpline scripts run in English. Describing a complex fraud in English, under stress, when you think in Hindi or Tamil or Marathi, is close to impossible. People give up before they start. Shame. Scammers are professionals running shift based operations with scripts for every response. They take money from software engineers, retired teachers, and homemakers alike. Victims blame themselves, stay quiet, and silence only protects the scammer. No clear first step. The information exists. It is scattered across portals, news articles, and WhatsApp forwards, none of which are open on your screen at the moment you need them. What Seerie does Seerie is a free Android app. It does four things, and it does them on your phone. Scan. Paste a suspicious SMS, share a screenshot, or hand it a PDF or a forwarded message. A sixteen layer rule engine checks it for the patterns that show up in Indian scams: UPI collect request bait, fake KYC deadlines, digital arrest scripts, job registration fees, OTP theft. You get a verdict, the specific red flags, and a numbered list of what to do next, in English and Hindi. Seerie Brain. An optional small language model that runs entirely on your device after a one time download over Wi-Fi. Ask it what a digital arrest call is, whether a job offer asking for a registration fee is normal, or what your scan result actually means. There is no cloud AI step. Your question does not leave your phone. Trusted SOS. Save up to two people. One tap sends them an alert from your own SIM, with your location if you choose to include it. If there is no signal, it falls back to WhatsApp, and then to a short range Bluetooth beacon. These alerts do not pass through our servers. Helplines. Cyber fraud 1930. Emergency 112. Women 181. Child 1098. One tap, no searching. There is also a moderated community thread for peer questions, and a safety playbook you can read offline and share with your family. Why we made it work offline This was the decision everything else followed from. An app that needs a connection is useless on a train, in a village with two bars of signal, or in the exact moment someone has panicked and handed over their phone. So the rule engine, the playbook, and the helplines work with the network off. The AI works offline too, once the model is downloaded. The second reason matters more. If scam checking happens on a server, then every suspicious message a user checks becomes data on a server. Bank SMS. Screenshots of private chats. Photographs of documents. We did not want to hold any of that, so we built it so that we cannot. Guest mode means you can install Seerie and use Home, Scan, Chat, and helplines without an account. Sign in only if you want community posting or history backup, and you can switch backup off entirely with local only mode. What Seerie is not We want to be exact about this, because safety tools that overclaim are dangerous. Seerie is not a government app. It is an independent education tool that points you toward official services. It is not one of them. Seerie is not legal or financial advice. For a specific case, confirm with your bank, the police, or a professional. Seerie does not replace 112 or 1930. For an emergency, call 112. For active fraud, call 1930 and file at cybercrime.gov.in. Seerie helps you get to those numbers faster and with the right information ready. Seerie Brain is a small model in beta. Treat it as a well informed friend, not an authority. Where this fits Seerie is the mobile piece of what we build at Seerror. The rest is browser and editor tooling with the same rule: the work happens on your machine. Seerguard scans your other Chrome extensions and scores them. Seerraze bulk deletes Discord history without touching our servers. Both are Chrome Web Store Featured with 5.0 ratings. Same idea each time. Useful privacy tools, free, with no data harvesting behind them. Try it Seerie is free on Google Play, with no ads and no paywall on core safety features. Download Seerie on Google Play More detail on how it works is at seerror.com/seerie.html . One ask. If you know someone who has been scammed, a parent, a colleague, a neighbour, send this to them. Not because they did anything wrong, but because they should know that help exists, it speaks their language, and it costs nothing. Cyber fraud helpline: 1930, available 24 hours. Sources: Ministry of Home Affairs Annual Report 2023–24, Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

content: Understanding retain : A New Way to Retain State in Jetpack Compose Richa Sharma 4 min read · Jul 25, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Is retain the beginning of the end for ViewModel ? Let's find out. Press enter or click to view image in full size credits — https://unsplash.com/ When Jetpack Compose was introduced, managing UI state became much simpler and more declarative. Depending on how long the state needs to survive and who owns it, Compose provides different solutions. The recommended approach was straightforward: remember :For Local UI State Use remember to store state that is local to a composable and only needs to survive recompositions. It's ideal for temporary UI interactions such as whether a dialog is visible, which tab is selected, or the current value of a text field. rememberSaveable : For State That Survives Configuration Changes When your UI state should persist across configuration changes like screen rotations or process recreation, rememberSaveable is the preferred choice. It automatically saves and restores values using the Android saved instance state mechanism, making it a great fit for simple, saveable data such as text input, scroll positions, or selected items. ViewModel : For Screen-Level State Management As applications grow, a screen often needs to manage more than just UI interactions. It may fetch data from a repository, handle user actions, perform asynchronous operations, and expose loading, success, or error states. This is where a ViewModel comes in. Rather than storing state inside the composable, the ViewModel acts as the screen-level state holder , surviving configuration changes while coordinating business logic and exposing observable UI state for Compose to render. Now, Compose Runtime introduces a new API called retain . Naturally, the Android community started asking: “Do we even need ViewModel anymore?” The answer isn’t a simple yes or no . Get Richa Sharma ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in In this article, we’ll explore: What retain is How it differs from remember How it compares with ViewModel When you should (and shouldn’t) use it Why wasn’t remember enough? Let’s start with a simple example. This works perfectly. Until -> Rotate the device. The state disappears.That’s because remember only survives recomposition .It does not survive the destruction and recreation of the Activity. We solved that using ViewModel Press enter or click to view image in full size Compose simply observes the ViewModel. The ViewModel survives configuration changes. Problem solved -> Or so we thought. Enter retain Compose Runtime now introduces a new concept. Instead of retaining Android components , it retains objects . Imagine writing: Instead of extending ViewModel , it's just a plain Kotlin class.Compose can retain this object across configuration changes. No Android lifecycle inheritance required. That’s the core idea behind retain . ViewModel belongs to AndroidX Lifecycle. Press enter or click to view image in full size With retain : Press enter or click to view image in full size Your state holder becomes independent of Android lifecycle classes. This makes it easier to: write reusable state holders share logic reduce framework coupling improve multiplatform compatibility Press enter or click to view image in full size Where retain shines Imagine a screen containing: Repository Use cases State Validation logic Previously you might create: Now you could simply write: No Android dependency -> Just Kotlin. Does this replace ViewModel? Not entirely -> ViewModel still provides several useful capabilities: viewModelScope SavedStateHandle Navigation integration Hilt support Lifecycle-aware cleanup If your screen relies on those features, ViewModel is still the right choice. retain doesn't automatically replace them. When should you use retain ? It’s a good fit when: Your state holder doesn’t need Android APIs. You want framework-independent business logic. You’re building reusable Compose components. You’re targeting Kotlin Multiplatform. When should you continue using ViewModel? Stick with ViewModel if you need: Navigation integration Hilt injection SavedStateHandle viewModelScope Existing architecture consistency Large Android apps will likely continue using ViewModel for many screens. Conclusion Jetpack Compose continues to move toward a more framework-independent architecture. retain is another step in that direction. Whether it becomes your default choice or remains a niche API, it’s worth understanding because it changes how we think about state ownership in Compose. As Compose evolves, we now have more flexibility than ever before. And that’s a good thing. content: Android Android App Development Android Development AndroidDev Android Xr The Complete Guide to Getting Started with Android XR Development Akshay Nandwana 16 min read · Jul 21, 2026 -- Listen Share A practical roadmap for Android developers Press enter or click to view image in full size A practical roadmap for Android developers — from your first emulator to spatial UI, 3D content, perception, and intelligent glasses Android development is no longer limited to the rectangular screen in your hand. With Android XR, developers can build applications that extend across spatial panels, immersive environments, XR headsets, wired glasses, audio glasses, and display glasses. Existing Android applications can continue running as traditional two-dimensional interfaces, while developers can progressively introduce spatial layouts, three-dimensional objects, real-world understanding, and hands-free interactions. The important part is this: You do not need to become a game developer before you can start building for Android XR. If you already understand Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Android Studio, lifecycle management, and adaptive layouts, you already have much of the foundation required. This guide explains what Android XR is, which tools you should choose, what concepts you should learn, and the order in which you should learn them. What exactly is Android XR? Android XR is an extension of the Android platform designed for a growing range of extended-reality devices. These devices currently fall into two broad experience categories: Immersive experiences These are primarily built for XR headsets and wired XR glasses. An immersive application can: Transport the user into a completely virtual environment Blend digital content with the physical world Place multiple application panels around the user Render interactive 3D objects Understand surfaces, depth, hands, faces, anchors, and device position Transition between traditional multitasking and a fully spatial experience Augmented experiences These are designed for devices such as audio glasses and display glasses. Instead of replacing the user’s surroundings, augmented experiences add lightweight information and assistance to everyday activities. Examples include: Live directions Translation Notifications Voice assistance Contextual information Checklists for field workers Navigation instructions Camera-assisted AI Hands-free communication Android XR supports both categories, but they involve different design constraints, device capabilities, and development libraries. The Android XR development landscape One of the first decisions you need to make is which development path fits your application. Android XR supports several familiar technologies: Jetpack XR SDK Kotlin and Jetpack Compose Android Views Unity Godot Unreal Engine OpenXR WebXR That flexibility is useful, but it can also make the starting point confusing. Here is a simple decision rule. Use Jetpack XR SDK when: You are already an Android developer You are extending an existing mobile or large-screen application Your application is primarily UI-driven You want to use Kotlin, Compose, Android architecture, and Jetpack You need spatial panels, 3D models, environments, or Android integrations You are building companion experiences for intelligent glasses Use Unity, Godot, or Unreal Engine when: Your application is primarily a game You need complex real-time 3D rendering Your team already has an existing engine-based XR project You need advanced physics, animation, shaders, or game-engine workflows Use OpenXR when: You need a lower-level, cross-platform XR standard You want greater control over rendering and device capabilities You are building an engine, framework, or deeply immersive application Use WebXR when: You are building a browser-based experience You want users to enter XR through a web page Your team is more familiar with web technologies than native Android For most existing Android developers, Jetpack XR SDK is the best first path . Android officially supports bringing existing mobile and large-screen applications into XR by spatializing familiar layouts and adding immersive capabilities incrementally. Phase 1: Strengthen your Android foundation Before touching an XR-specific API, make sure you are comfortable with the following Android concepts: Kotlin Coroutines and Flow Jetpack Compose State management Android lifecycle ViewModel Material Design Adaptive layouts Navigation Permissions Media and camera APIs Android Virtual Devices You do not need to master every Android API. However, Jetpack Compose is particularly important because the official Android XR fundamentals codelabs are Compose-based. Google recommends prior experience with Kotlin, Compose, Android Studio, and virtual devices before starting them. A developer who can already create a Compose application, manage UI state, and run it on an emulator is ready to begin. Phase 2: Understand the Android XR device categories Do not treat “XR” as a single device type. Android XR supports: XR headsets These provide a wide field of view and can create fully immersive virtual environments. Typical inputs include: Hand tracking Eye tracking Motion controllers Gaze Voice Mouse and keyboard Wired XR glasses These can provide spatial and immersive experiences while being connected to another computing device. They may support: Spatial UI Passthrough Real-world anchoring Hand and eye input High-quality visual content Audio glasses These may not have a visual display. Experiences are driven through sound, speech, sensors, notifications, and AI assistance. Display glasses These provide lightweight visual information over the user’s real-world view. Their interfaces must be minimal, readable, glanceable, and comfortable. Android provides Jetpack Compose Glimmer , a Compose-based toolkit specifically optimized for display-glasses experiences. title: How Many Trees Does Your Framework Need?
excerpt: Three jobs every UI framework must staff: configuration, identity, behavior — and three different org charts: Views hire one object for everything, Compose splits bookkeeping from physics, Flutter gives each job its own tree. Android Native vs KMP vs Flutter — a series comparing how the three mobile stacks solve the same problems differently. Part 4: the data structures behind the pixels. content: Android Kotlin Multiplatform Jetpack Compose Flutter How Many Trees Does Your Framework Need? Angelina Andronova 5 min read · Jul 26, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Three jobs every UI framework must staff: configuration, identity, behavior — and three different org charts: Views hire one object for everything, Compose splits bookkeeping from physics, Flutter gives each job its own tree. Android Native vs KMP vs Flutter — a series comparing how the three mobile stacks solve the same problems differently. Part 4: the data structures behind the pixels. Put a button on screen and ask what the framework must remember to keep it alive. Three things, it turns out. What you asked for: the text, the color, the padding: call it the configuration . Which button this is, the same one as last frame, still holding its ripple animation and its focus: call it the identity . And someone has to do the physical labor: measure, position, paint: call it the behavior . Three jobs. Every UI framework hires for all three. The question that explains almost everything else about Android Views, Jetpack Compose, and Flutter is a staffing decision: how many trees do you employ to cover three jobs? Views answer one. Compose answers two. Flutter answers three. None of these numbers is an accident. One tree: Android Views A View is all three jobs in a single object. Its fields are the configuration. The object itself is the identity; it stays alive as long as it’s attached, which is why it can privately hold a scroll position. And the behavior is its own methods: onMeasure , onLayout , onDraw . The benefit is a mental model you can hold in one hand: the UI is a tree of objects, and changing the UI means calling setters on it. The charge appears at scale. Because every node carries everything, every node is heavy: expensive to create (there’s a reason we say “inflate”), expensive enough to keep that the platform grew a whole recycling industry around list rows. And since the current screen is the sum of every setter ever called, there is no record of how you got here: no second copy to compare against, nothing to replay. Mutation happens in place, and in place it stays. One tree, three hats, no history. Two trees: Jetpack Compose Compose splits the staff asymmetrically: bookkeeping in one structure, behavior in another. The bookkeeping lives in the slot table , a record of the last composition: which composable ran, at which position, with which parameters, and what it remember ed. When state changes, Compose doesn't diff two trees; it re-runs only the functions subscribed to that state and patches the record in place. Here’s the part that surprised me: the slot table is a tree that doesn’t look like one. It’s stored as two flat arrays: an IntArray of groups and an Object[] of slots, laid out in depth-first order, like a diary of the run. Each group records the size of its own subtree, so "skip my children" is not a walk, it's index += span . Parent and child are recovered by arithmetic, the way a binary heap keeps a whole tree inside a plain array and nobody complains it isn't one. The shape is a tree; the storage is a trace. Composition replays linearly, so the natural format for its memory is linear too, and an IntArray allocates no objects for the garbage collector to chase. The behavior lives in the LayoutNode tree , real, long-lived objects this time, one per emitted layout, each holding its measure policy and its chain of modifiers. This is the tree that actually does the physics. The only bridge between the two structures is a pointer stored in the slot table: this group built that node . On recomposition, Compose finds the group by position, follows the pointer, and runs a few setters on the existing node. Nothing is rebuilt. Press enter or click to view image in full size The Compose machine, step by step: the slot table (bookkeeping) builds the LayoutNode tree (behavior), and one real View carries the frame into Android’s classic pipeline. Interactive version: angelinaballerina11.github.io/compose-two-trees And then, the exit ramp. All of this machinery lives inside exactly one classic Android View. When a frame arrives, the old pipeline calls onMeasure and dispatchDraw on it like on any button, and Compose does its measuring and drawing inside those calls. Compose owns its trees; Android still owns the last mile to the screen. Three trees: Flutter Flutter takes the split further, and adds a philosophy of its own: configurations should be so cheap you can throw them all away, every frame, without guilt. Get Angelina Andronova ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Widgets are the configuration: immutable descriptions with no size, no position, no lifecycle. Every rebuild produces brand-new widget objects, even for the parts that didn’t change. That sounds wasteful until you see what it buys. Elements are the identity: the persistent spine that survives every rebuild. Each Element compares the old widget in its hand to the new one: same type, same key? Then nothing structural happened: keep everything, swap the description, move on. The State objects hang off Elements too, which is the entire trick of setState : state survives because its host Element survives, while widgets die around it by design. RenderObjects are the behavior: the heavyweight machines that measure with constraints-down-sizes-up and paint into layers. Only some widgets employ one; the render tree is always much smaller than the other two. When a diff finds a changed property, the Element calls updateRenderObject : same machine, new setting, exactly like Compose patching its LayoutNode. Press enter or click to view image in full size Flutter’s three trees in motion: throwaway Widgets, the persistent Element spine, RenderObjects doing the physics, rasterized by Flutter’s own engine. content: Android Accessibility Material Design Android App Development UI Dissecting Expanded Dark Theme with Claude Science and AOSP Aryan K 6 min read · 6 days ago -- 1 Listen Share There’s a lot of excitement around customization, personalization, accessibility, and giving people more control over how interfaces adapt to their needs. I’m interested in what happens underneath, and dark mode hides a surprising amount of engineering. A dark theme is more than a binary inversion. Colors can change, but the visual cues and relationships that give an interface meaning still need to carry through. Dark mode might feel like a preference for some people, but it can matter much more for those with low vision or photosensitivity. Press enter or click to view image in full size The Android robot comparing light and dark themes. Image generated by author. For years, whether an app on your phone had dark mode depended on whether its developers built one. Android 10 (2019) introduced Force Dark , letting developers hand that work off to Android, which could generate a dark version from the app’s existing light theme. Then in late 2025, an Android 16 update introduced Expanded Dark Theme , putting that choice in users’ hands. Users can now ask Android to darken apps that still showed up light, even when those apps never provided their own dark theme. That shift toward user agency caught my attention. I used Claude Science to probe Expanded Dark Theme: I built a light-only Android app, measured what changed across common interface patterns, and traced the results back through Android’s rendering code. Setup I tested fourteen interface patterns on one screen, in three versions. The original light theme, the dark version Android generated from it (I’ll call it auto-dark), and a dark theme I built by hand following Material 3 , Google’s own design system (hand-built). Press enter or click to view image in full size Left to Right: Light mode, Android’s Expanded Dark Theme (auto-dark), and a hand-built Material 3 dark theme What Android preserved Could the transformation take readable text and make it unreadable? No. In my experiment, everything that passed the WCAG contrast floor in light mode still passed after darkening, and everything I deliberately built broken stayed broken. The ratio behind those verdicts is: Contrast Ratio = (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05) where L is each color’s relative luminance. White text on the orange banner failed at 2.8 in light mode and 2.7 in auto-dark. Android inherited my accessibility contrasts rather than auditing or changing them. Color families held too, for the most part. Blues stayed blue, reds stayed red. The one exception was the orange banner, which came out red. The reason turned out to be buried in the rendering code, which comes later. Press enter or click to view image in full size Auto-dark mostly preserved color families. The orange brand color was the exception, shifting toward red The next question I had was how close an automatic dark theme gets to one a person actually designed. Automatic vs hand-built On plain text and surfaces, the auto-dark theme came remarkably close to the hand-built one, with only minor color differences. On these simpler patterns, the OS came surprisingly close to my hand-built output without seeing a single design token. The gap surfaced in colorful, mid-toned elements (think link, errors, search, and banner); all read 1.8 to 2.5 times better when hand-built. The brand banner shows the difference. My hand-built Material theme never touched the original orange. It stretched the brand color into a palette of tones, then picked tones by the banner’s role, so the dark scheme gave it a deep brown fill with pale peach text, the orange’s own dark and light ends, passing contrast at 6.6 to 1 by design. Get Aryan K ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in These role labels, assigned by a developer, never reach Android’s renderer. In the auto-dark case, the banner is just a color, so all Android can do is run it through the darkening math, and it came out at 2.7 to 1 and redder. Press enter or click to view image in full size Auto-dark ties the hand-built theme on plain text and loses on colored elements, by 1.8 to 2.5 times Press enter or click to view image in full size Contrast ratios for the nine cleanly measured patterns against the WCAG thresholds The failures clustered around saturated colors and middle grays. To understand why those colors behaved differently, I traced how Android transforms them in the renderer. Inside the renderer For ordinary Android UI rendering, the app records drawing instructions that eventually pass through HWUI, Android’s hardware-accelerated UI renderer. Expanded Dark Theme can transform colors in those drawing instructions before they become pixels. Press enter or click to view image in full size Expanded Dark Theme sits between an app’s drawing instructions and the pixels Roughly, Android first decides whether a rendered chunk behaves like foreground or background. Text-containing nodes tend to become foreground and get pushed lighter; backgrounds get pushed darker, and the background guess is a heuristic the source itself labels a crude overlap check . Then one small piece of math picks the new color: new lightness = min(110 − old lightness, 100) applied only when it moves in the right direction. That guard is why my mid-grays never moved; a gray at lightness 50 maps to 60, wrong direction, left alone. Left alone is the trap. The gray stays put while everything behind it goes black, which is why the hand-built theme beat auto-dark on my placeholder; a designer re-lightens that gray, and the math never does.
