title: 11/28: The Compositor You’ve Never Seen Is Drawing Your App
excerpt: SurfaceFlinger, BufferQueue, and how pixels reach the screen Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android Development Aosp Graphics Android Kotlin 11/28: The Compositor You’ve Never Seen Is Drawing Your App Pramod Patel 7 min read · 5 days ago -- 1 Listen Share SurfaceFlinger, BufferQueue, and how pixels reach the screen Press enter or click to view image in full size Your app renders into a Surface and hands the buffer to a BufferQueue . A separate process, SurfaceFlinger , consumes those buffers, composites every visible surface into one frame, and sends it to the display. Your app never touches the screen. Your app has never once drawn a pixel to the screen. Not in any app you’ve ever shipped. A separate process you’ve probably never heard of does that, and your job was only ever to hand it a buffer. I believed the opposite for years. I pictured onDraw putting ink on glass, my Canvas calls landing directly on the display. That mental model is wrong in a way that matters, because it hides the entire final mile of rendering: the part that explains why your app appears layered under the status bar you never drew, why screenshots capture system UI your process can't see, and why "double buffering" is a thing anyone ever had to invent. Follow your frame past the edge of your own process. What happens to your frame after doFrame? Last episode ended with Choreographer.doFrame running your traversal (measure, layout, draw) on the vsync tick. The output of all that work is a single rendered buffer : a chunk of graphics memory with your frame's pixels in it. That buffer lives in a Surface . And the framework is refreshingly blunt about what a Surface actually is: Press enter or click to view image in full size Surface on cs.android.com. The very first line of the class doc: "Handle onto a raw buffer that is being managed by the screen compositor." It then spells out the model: a Surface is created from a consumer of buffers and handed to a producer that draws into it. You are the producer. Read that javadoc twice. Your Surface is not the screen. It's a handle onto a raw buffer , and that buffer is "managed by the screen compositor," some other entity that owns the real display. The doc even names the roles: a Surface comes from a consumer of image buffers and is handed to a producer to draw into. When your app renders, you are the producer. You fill a buffer. You do not display it. For software rendering, you can see the handoff directly in the Surface API: // frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/Surface.java public Canvas lockCanvas(Rect inOutDirty) { /* ... */ mLockedObject = nativeLockCanvas(mNativeObject, mCanvas, inOutDirty); return mCanvas; } public void unlockCanvasAndPost(Canvas canvas) { /* ... */ // posts the new contents of the Canvas to the surface } lockCanvas dequeues a buffer from a queue and hands you a Canvas to paint on. unlockCanvasAndPost queues the finished buffer back. (Hardware-accelerated rendering does the same dance through the HWUI render thread and eglSwapBuffers , but the shape is identical: dequeue, draw, queue.) That "post" is the moment your pixels leave your control. Where do they go? What’s the pipe between you and the compositor? A BufferQueue , and its design is the whole mechanism in one class. Look at how you even get one: Press enter or click to view image in full size BufferQueue on cs.android.com ( frameworks/native ). You can't construct one directly: BufferQueue() = delete . You call createBufferQueue(outProducer, outConsumer, ...) , which hands back two endpoints : an IGraphicBufferProducer and an IGraphicBufferConsumer . One queue, two ends, two owners. This is the producer/consumer pattern, made concrete in graphics memory. createBufferQueue returns two interfaces: IGraphicBufferProducer : goes to your app. You dequeue an empty buffer, render into it, and queue it back. IGraphicBufferConsumer : goes to SurfaceFlinger . It acquires filled buffers and releases them when done. The two ends live in different processes , and the buffers themselves are shared graphics memory (gralloc) passed by handle, not copied. That’s the elegance: your app and the compositor never block on each other or memcpy a full frame; they pass ownership of buffers around a ring. Your unlockCanvasAndPost queued a buffer onto the producer end; somewhere across a process boundary, a consumer is waiting to pick it up. So who is the consumer? A process named SurfaceFlinger , which boots with the system and runs for the life of the device: Press enter or click to view image in full size SurfaceFlinger on cs.android.com ( frameworks/native/services/surfaceflinger ). Note what it extends: BnSurfaceComposer , a Binder native stub (Episode 6). SurfaceFlinger is a Binder service, a separate system process, and it is the consumer on the other end of your BufferQueue . That BnSurfaceComposer base class should look familiar after Episode 5 and Episode 6 : the Bn prefix is the native-side Binder stub, the C++ cousin of the AIDL Stub . SurfaceFlinger is a system service you talk to over Binder, and it is the consumer of every app's buffers. Your queue isn't the only one feeding it. Every visible thing on screen has its own surface and its own BufferQueue pointed at SurfaceFlinger. What does SurfaceFlinger actually do with all those buffers? It composites. On each display refresh, it takes the latest queued buffer from every visible surface (your app, the status bar, the navigation bar, the wallpaper, an overlay or two) and blends them into one final image in the correct z-order: Press enter or click to view image in full size What “your app on screen” really is. SurfaceFlinger takes one buffer from each visible surface and composites them, respecting layering and transparency, into the single frame the display shows. The status bar you never drew is a different app’s buffer, blended in beside yours. content: Abstract Classes vs Interfaces in Kotlin: Understanding the Right Choice Tech Dynasty 5 min read · Jul 26, 2026 -- Listen Share As your Kotlin applications grow, you’ll often need multiple classes to share common behavior. For example, different payment methods should all be able to process payments, various screens should support loading states, and different animals should make their own sounds. Kotlin provides two powerful tools for solving these problems: Abstract Classes and Interfaces . Press enter or click to view image in full size Although they may seem similar at first, they serve different purposes. Choosing the right one can make your code cleaner, more flexible, and easier to maintain. In this article, we’ll explore what abstract classes and interfaces are, how they differ, when to use each one, and how they’re used in real-world Android development. Why Do We Need Abstraction? Imagine you’re building a food delivery application. Every payment method should support: Processing payments Cancelling payments However, each payment type behaves differently. Credit Card UPI Net Banking Wallet Writing the same functions in every class leads to duplicated code. Instead, define a common contract that all payment methods must follow. This is the purpose of abstraction. What Is an Abstract Class? An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated directly . It serves as a base class that provides: Common properties Common functions Shared implementation Abstract functions that child classes must implement Think of it as a partially completed blueprint. Creating an Abstract Class abstract class Animal { abstract fun makeSound() } This class cannot be instantiated. val animal = Animal() Compilation error. Instead, another class must inherit from it. Implementing an Abstract Class abstract class Animal { abstract fun makeSound() } Child class: class Dog : Animal() { override fun makeSound() { println("Bark") } } Usage: val dog = Dog() dog.makeSound() Output: Bark Abstract Classes Can Have Implementations Unlike interfaces, abstract classes can contain both abstract and concrete members. abstract class Employee { fun login() { println("Employee Logged In") } abstract fun work() } Child: class Developer : Employee() { override fun work() { println("Writing Kotlin Code") } } Usage: val developer = Developer() developer.login() developer.work() Output: Employee Logged In Writing Kotlin Code What Is an Interface? An interface defines a contract that classes agree to implement. It specifies what a class should do , not how it should do it . Interfaces are ideal for describing capabilities. Examples: Clickable Draggable Payable Downloadable Creating an Interface interface Payment { fun pay() } Any class implementing this interface must provide its own implementation. Implementing an Interface interface Payment { fun pay() } class CardPayment : Payment { override fun pay() { println("Paid using Card") } } Usage: val payment = CardPayment() payment.pay() Output: Paid using Card Interfaces Can Have Default Implementations Kotlin interfaces aren’t limited to abstract methods. They can also contain implemented functions. interface Logger { fun log(message: String) { println(message) } } Classes automatically inherit this implementation unless they choose to override it. Multiple Interface Implementation One of the biggest advantages of interfaces is that a class can implement multiple interfaces. interface Camera { fun capture() } interface MusicPlayer { fun playMusic() } Implementation: class Smartphone : Camera, MusicPlayer { override fun capture() { println("Taking Photo") } override fun playMusic() { println("Playing Music") } } Unlike classes, Kotlin allows multiple interface implementation. Abstract Class vs Interface Let’s compare them. Press enter or click to view image in full size When Should You Use an Abstract Class? Choose an abstract class when: Multiple classes share common state. Multiple classes share implementation. Child classes have a strong “is-a” relationship. You need constructors. You want to reuse code. Example: Vehicle │ ├── Car ├── Bike └── Bus Every vehicle has: Speed Fuel Engine These shared characteristics belong naturally in an abstract base class. When Should You Use an Interface? Use an interface when classes simply share a capability. Example: Payable Implemented by: CardPayment UpiPayment WalletPayment These classes don’t share common state, but they all know how to perform a payment. Another example: Clickable Implemented by: Button ImageView CardView Real-World Android Examples RecyclerView Click Listener interface OnItemClickListener { fun onItemClick(position: Int) } Activities and fragments implement this interface to respond to item clicks. ViewModel Base Class abstract class BaseViewModel { fun showLoading() { println("Loading...") } } All ViewModels inherit the common loading behavior. Payment System interface Payment { fun pay() } class UpiPayment : Payment { override fun pay() { println("Paid using UPI") } } class CardPayment : Payment { override fun pay() { println("Paid using Card") } } Each payment method fulfills the same contract with its own implementation. Media Player interface Playable { fun play() } interface Downloadable { fun download() } class Song : Playable, Downloadable { override fun play() { println("Playing Song") } override fun download() { println("Downloading Song") } } The Song class demonstrates how a class can have multiple capabilities through interfaces. Best Practices When designing Kotlin applications: Use an abstract class when classes share state and implementation. Use an interface to define capabilities or behavior. Prefer interfaces when multiple unrelated classes need the same functionality. Use abstract classes for strong inheritance relationships. Keep interfaces focused on a single responsibility. Avoid large “god interfaces” with too many methods. Favor composition and interfaces over deep inheritance hierarchie

title: Thinking Like the Compose Runtime
excerpt: Part 2 — If Composable Functions Keep Running, How Do They Remember Anything? Continue reading on Medium »
content: Jetpack Compose Android App Development Android Kotlin Kotlin Multiplatform Thinking Like the Compose Runtime Neeraja Gandla 5 min read · Jul 26, 2026 -- Listen Share Part 2 — If Composable Functions Keep Running, How Do They Remember Anything? Press enter or click to view image in full size In the previous part, we made a bold decision. Instead of manually updating every TextView , Button , and ProgressBar , we asked a much simpler question. What if the UI was nothing more than a function of state? That single idea changed everything. Instead of updating the UI ourselves, we would update the application’s state. The runtime would do the rest. No more manually synchronizing dozens of views. No more wondering whether we forgot to hide a loading spinner or update a toolbar title. The UI would always be a reflection of the latest state. It felt elegant. It felt simple. It felt like we’d finally solved the problem. Until someone in the room asked a question that brought the entire discussion to a halt. “If the runtime keeps executing these composable functions… how do they remember anything?” Silence. Because every engineer in the room knew the answer. Functions don’t remember. Let’s Build Compose Ourselves Forget that remember exists. Forget the Compose Runtime. Imagine it’s 2018. Google has asked you to help design the next Android UI toolkit. You begin with the simplest possible composable. @Composable fun CounterScreen(count: Int) { Text("Count: $count") } Our runtime has only one responsibility. Whenever the state changes… execute the function again. count = 0 ↓ CounterScreen(0) ↓ count = 1 ↓ CounterScreen(1) ↓ count = 2 ↓ CounterScreen(2) So far, life is wonderfully simple. Every new state produces a new UI. Exactly what we wanted. Now let’s build something that behaves a little more like a real application. A Screen That Users Can Interact With Imagine the screen allows the user to expand and collapse a details section. @Composable fun CounterScreen(count: Int) { var expanded = false Column { Text("Count: $count") Button( onClick = { expanded = !expanded } ) { Text( if (expanded) "Hide Details" else "Show Details" ) } if (expanded) { Details() } } } Let’s walk through what happens. The screen appears. expanded is false . The details are hidden. The user taps Show Details . expanded becomes true . The details appear. Everything behaves exactly as the user expects. Now imagine something completely unrelated happens. Perhaps a timer ticks. Perhaps a network response arrives. Perhaps another piece of state changes. Our counter increases. count 0 ↓ 1 Nothing about the details section changed. The user didn’t touch it. They didn’t collapse it. They didn’t navigate away. Only the counter changed. According to the rule we established in Part 1, the runtime executes CounterScreen() again. The function starts from the very beginning. var expanded = false Again. The details disappear. The user loses the state they just created. If this happened in a real application, we’d call it a bug. But the bug isn’t in our code. The bug is in our design. Our runtime has no way of remembering what happened before. The Problem Isn’t Compose It’s Functions. Let’s step away from Compose for a moment. Consider a perfectly ordinary Kotlin function. fun greet(name: String) { println("Hello $name") } Suppose I asked you a strange question. How many times has this function been called? You can’t answer it. Not because Kotlin is missing a feature. Because that’s simply not what functions do. A function begins executing. It creates local variables. It performs its work. It returns. Everything inside it disappears. Get Neeraja Gandla ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in The next invocation starts with a completely clean slate. Composable functions obey exactly the same rules. They’re still ordinary Kotlin functions. So why are we expecting them to behave differently? Because users don’t think in terms of function calls. They think in terms of screens. When a screen updates, users expect the things they did a moment ago to still be there. They expect: the expanded section to remain expanded, the entered text to remain entered, the selected tab to remain selected, the scroll position to remain exactly where they left it. In other words… users expect the UI to have memory. Functions don’t. An Impossible Requirement At this point, imagine you’re one of the engineers designing Compose. Someone writes two requirements on the whiteboard. Requirement 1 Composable functions should behave like ordinary Kotlin functions. Requirement 2 Composable functions should remember values from previous executions. Everyone stares at the board. Those two requirements contradict each other. Unless… we’ve been asking the wrong question. We’ve been asking: How can a function remember something? Maybe the better question is: Who said the function has to remember at all? That tiny change in perspective changes everything. The First Wrong Solution Let’s try the obvious approach. Move the state outside the function. var expanded = false @Composable fun CounterScreen(count: Int) { Button( onClick = { expanded = !expanded } ) { Text("Toggle") } if (expanded) { Details() } } Problem solved? Let’s find out. Imagine we display two counters. CounterScreen(count = 5) CounterScreen(count = 42) Now expand the first one. The second one expands too. Why? Because both composables are reading the same global variable. We’ve fixed one problem by creating another. Global state clearly isn’t the answer. The Second Wrong Solution Fine. Let’s keep the state inside the function. Except… that’s exactly where we started. The function finishes executing. Its local variables disappear. The next execution starts from scratch. There is nowhere inside the function to keep yesterday’s values. We’re stuck. And that’s a good sign. Because when every obvious solution fails, it usually m

content: RustRover Focus on what matters Follow Follow: X X Download All News Releases How do you rewrite C/C++ projects to Rust? Irina Mihajlovic Disclaimer: This article was created with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the JetBrains RustRover team. C and C++ to Rust migrations are no longer just an experimental idea. More teams are now looking at Rust as a practical way to improve memory safety, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and modernize performance-critical systems. But a successful migration is not about rewriting everything just because Rust is popular. The hard question is more practical: ‘’Why should teams consider Rust for existing C or C++ systems, which parts of those systems should move to Rust, and how do you do it without breaking what already works?’’ This was one of the main topics in our recent livestream with Luca Palmieri from Mainmatter , author of 100 Exercises To Learn Rust and the upcoming C to Rust Migration book , and Vitaly Bragilevsky from JetBrains. Mainmatter works with teams adopting Rust in real-world software projects, including through consulting, training, and migration support. In the livestream, Luca Palmieri shared what that practical experience shows: where C and C++ to Rust migration projects succeed, where they usually get stuck, and why incremental migration is often the safer path. The full livestream is available here: Tldr: For many production systems, the safest C++-to Rust migration strategy is not a full rewrite. It is an incremental migration: start with isolated modules, make Rust work inside the existing build and release process, and expand gradually as confidence grows. Related resources: Mainmatter offers Rust consulting for teams planning or running migration projects.  For a deeper look at migration patterns, check out Mainmatter’s C to Rust Migration book . And if your team wants to strengthen its Rust foundations first, Luca Palmieri’s 100 Exercises To Learn Rust is available as a JetBrains Academy course. Why teams are migrating from C and C++ to Rust A few years ago, suggesting a C or C++ to Rust migration could feel risky. Nobody wants to be the canary in the coal mine, especially when the project is load-bearing, serving production traffic, or important to the business. If a team is investing years of engineering effort into a migration, they need to know they will not discover a roadblock halfway through. That hesitation is weaker today. Companies like Google aren’t just migrating to Rust; they’re publishing data arguing that Rust adoption improves safety , especially by reducing memory-safety vulnerabilities, and reducing defect rates compared to their C++ predecessors. Beyond de-risking, there are several factors that have had an impact on today’s situation: Expertise is spreading. Engineers who learned Rust at one company bring that knowledge to their next role, creating a multiplier effect across the industry. Tooling has matured. The ecosystem gaps that made early adoption painful have largely been filled. Hiring concerns are fading. The argument that “we can’t find Rust developers” loses substance when more developers have production Rust experience. AI assistance reduces friction. Generative AI tools help flatten the learning curve, making the initial ramp-up less daunting. The question has changed. Teams are now asking whether their C or C++ codebase has a problem that looks like a good fit for Rust. For a broader look at how the two languages compare, including memory safety, performance, and concurrency, see our Rust vs C++ comparison . Let’s see which projects should migrate and how. Which Projects Should Migrate? Not every C or C++ project benefits from a Rust migration. For hobby projects, the calculus is simple: migrate if you want to learn Rust or if it feels right. For production systems, migration needs to make business sense. The strongest candidates are usually codebases where maintainability is already expensive: Performance-sensitive codebases where squeezing every ounce of efficiency pushes teams toward complex patterns that are hard to reason about. Rust’s safety guarantees don’t compromise performance, but they do make those complex patterns more manageable. Concurrent or multi-threaded systems where the borrow checker provides safety nets that are difficult to replicate in C++. Data races and memory safety issues that require constant vigilance in C++ become compile-time errors in Rust. Security-critical components where vulnerabilities carry high costs. If your code is an attractive attack target, preventing memory safety issues before they reach production has clear economic value. High-scale deployments where even modest efficiency improvements translate to meaningful infrastructure savings. If migrating to Rust lets you run on less powerful hardware, those savings compound quickly. The common thread is maintainability. Successful migrations improve the ability to ship features faster, reduce defect rates, or both. The migration cost must be justified by reduced rework, fewer security incidents, improved developer productivity, or operational savings. C++ to Rust migration: Full Rewrite vs. Incremental Migration The choice between a complete rewrite and an incremental migration isn’t ideological. It depends on your deployment model, codebase characteristics, and available testing infrastructure. A full rewrite can sound appealing. You start from scratch, set up the codebase the way you want, draw the boundaries where you like, and leave old decisions behind. But let’s see where a full rewrite makes sense? When Full Rewrites C/C++ to Rust Make Sense The codebase is relatively small, and the scope is tractable You have an exhaustive black-box test suite that validates behavior without assuming internal structure The API surface is well-defined and stable You control the deployment environment Services deployed as backends can be good candidates. You can route shadow traffic to the new implementation

title: The Ultimate Guide to Kotlin Coroutine Builders for Android Developers
excerpt: ReadMore https://leanpub.com/master_coroutine_flow Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Android Development Kotlin Coroutines Jetpack Programming The Ultimate Guide to Kotlin Coroutine Builders for Android Developers Mahmoud Ramadan 10 min read · 4 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size ReadMore https://leanpub.com/master_coroutine_flow A coroutine doesn’t start itself. Something has to bridge from regular code into the suspending world and kick it off. That something is a builder . This chapter is a tour of every builder you’ll use, and — more importantly — the decision rules for choosing among them. 3.1 What a Builder Is A coroutine builder is a function that takes a block of suspending code and starts a coroutine to run it. It’s the doorway between the non-suspending world (regular functions, lifecycle callbacks, click listeners) and the suspending world (everything that can call delay , fetchUser , and friends). We met three builders in Chapter 2 without naming them as a family. Let’s name them now, plus the ones we haven’t seen: BuilderReturnsBlocks caller?Primary use launchJob NoFire-and-forget work asyncDeferred<T> NoConcurrent work that returns a value runBlockingT Yes Bridging blocking code → suspend (main, tests) withContextT No (suspends)Switching dispatcher within a coroutine coroutineScopeT No (suspends)Grouping child coroutines safely supervisorScopeT No (suspends)Like coroutineScope , isolated child failures The first three start coroutines from outside the coroutine world. The last three are called from inside a coroutine and are technically “scoping functions” rather than launchers — but they’re built on the same machinery and you reach for them constantly, so they belong in this tour. We’ll cover the first three in depth here and introduce the scoping functions, then go deep on scope and context in Chapter 4 and structured concurrency in Chapter 5. 3.2 launch in Depth launch starts a coroutine that runs concurrently and returns a Job — a handle to that running coroutine. It does not return the result of the block; the block's return value is discarded. val job: Job = scope.launch { val user = fetchUser("1") saveToDatabase(user) } The Job is your control surface for that coroutine. The operations you'll actually use: job.cancel()          // request cancellation job.join()            // suspend until the coroutine finishes (or is cancelled) job.isActive          // true while running job.isCompleted       // true once finished job.isCancelled       // true if cancelled job.invokeOnCompletion { cause -> /* cleanup */ }  // callback when it ends join() is worth highlighting: it lets one coroutine wait for another to finish without caring about its result. If you find yourself wanting both "wait for it" and "get its value," you wanted async / await , not launch / join . Start modes launch (and async ) accept a start parameter that controls when the coroutine actually begins: val job = scope.launch(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { expensiveSetup() } // nothing has run yet job.start()   // now it begins // or: job.join() / the first await() also triggers a LAZY coroutine CoroutineStart.DEFAULT — starts immediately (almost always what you want). CoroutineStart.LAZY — doesn't start until you call start() , join() , or await() . Useful when you want to create a coroutine now but trigger it later. CoroutineStart.ATOMIC and UNDISPATCHED exist for advanced cases (controlling cancellation timing and initial dispatch); you'll rarely need them, and we'll flag them where relevant rather than dwelling here. In day-to-day Android code, you’ll use the default and never pass start at all. Know LAZY exists; reach for it when you genuinely want deferred triggering. 3.3 async in Depth async starts a coroutine and returns a Deferred<T> , which is a Job that also carries a future result. Everything true of Job is true of Deferred — you can cancel it, join it, check isActive — plus you can await() its value. val deferred: Deferred<User> = scope.async { fetchUser("1") } // Deferred IS-A Job: deferred.cancel()         // valid val user = deferred.await() // and additionally: get the result The Chapter 2 lesson bears repeating because it’s the single most misused thing about async : async is for concurrency, not for "calling a suspend function." If you write async { x() }.await() with nothing in between, delete the async and just call x() . The value of async is starting several pieces of independent work before awaiting any of them: suspend fun loadDashboard(): Dashboard = coroutineScope { val profile = async { fetchProfile() } val feed = async { fetchFeed() } val notifications = async { fetchNotifications() } Dashboard(profile.await(), feed.await(), notifications.await()) // all three ran concurrently; total time ≈ the slowest one } Exception timing differs from launch There’s a subtle but important behavioral difference. A launch coroutine throws its exception immediately (propagating to its scope / CoroutineExceptionHandler ). An async coroutine holds its exception until you await() it: val deferred = scope.async { throw IllegalStateException("boom") } // nothing thrown yet... deferred.await()  // ⬅ the exception surfaces HERE This means an async result you never await can swallow a failure silently. It's another reason not to use async for fire-and-forget work — launch surfaces problems when they happen. We'll treat exception propagation rigorously in Chapter 8; for now, internalize: launch throws eagerly, async throws on await . 3.4 runBlocking — the Bridge You Rarely Want runBlocking runs a coroutine and blocks the current thread until it completes, then returns the block's result. It is the inverse of every other builder: instead of freeing the thread, it ties the thread up. fun main() { val result = runBlocking {   // blocks main thread of this CLI program fetchUser("1") } println(result) } Its legitimate uses are narrow: main() in a CLI app — you need somewhere to start, and blocking the process's main thread is fine because there's no

title: How We Built an MCP Server in Kotlin — Keeping Stdio Clean for JSON-RPC
excerpt: I didn’t want to learn a new runtime to ship a tool for an AI agent. Continue reading on Level Up Coding »
content: Kotlin Mcp Server AI Productivity Android Kotlin · MCP · Developer Tools How We Built an MCP Server in Kotlin — Keeping Stdio Clean for JSON-RPC Joseph Sanjaya 7 min read · 5 days ago -- 1 Listen Share I didn’t want to learn a new runtime to ship a tool for an AI agent. I’m a Kotlin engineer. Coroutines, @Serializable data classes, Gradle modules, fat JARs — that's the stack I think in. When agents started showing up in editors and asking for tools, my first instinct wasn't to reach for Node or Python. It was to check whether Kotlin could close the loop. So I built gradle-opt-mcp — a server that gives Claude direct access to your Gradle build: dependency graphs, cache health, build scans, test summaries, all without pasting logs by hand. The official Kotlin MCP SDK is real, actively maintained, and idiomatic. The stdio transport that Cursor, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code all use maps cleanly to a main function and a suspend-friendly server. Your @Serializable data classes become tool schemas. Your coroutines become the handler model. The fat JAR you already know how to build becomes the process the editor spawns. One Android instinct killed my first session before a single tool call completed — and I didn’t know I had it until it broke. stdout is the JSON-RPC socket. Every byte you write to it is protocol. That’s the only new rule. Everything else is Kotlin you already know. What the Process Actually Looks Like Forget Ktor-on-a-port for a minute. On the stdio transport, the MCP client owns your process entirely. Cursor, Claude Desktop, or Claude Code runs java -jar your-server.jar . Your main starts. Stdin becomes the incoming socket. Stdout becomes the outgoing socket. The parent process holds both ends of the pipe. The handshake is deliberately boring. The client sends initialize . You respond with your server name, version, and declared capabilities. The client confirms with notifications/initialized . Then tools/list arrives, you answer with your catalog, and from there it's a stream of tools/call frames until stdin closes. When stdin closes, you exit. Hang a thread and the editor is stuck with a process that can’t answer calls and won’t die. That’s the entire runtime shape: one process tied to one editor session, with stdin and stdout as the only socket. The moment that picture is clear, the stdout rule stops feeling like a constraint. The wire was never yours to use. The Instinct That Kills the Session Kotlin engineers log to stdout. Not consciously — it’s just what println does, and on Android, Logback routes everything to logcat where it belongs and nothing breaks. On stdio transport, it breaks immediately. Ten minutes into my work, Cursor completely froze with no error message. When I ran the JAR manually and piped in an initialize frame, the response died mid-parse. It turns out a single line of Logback startup noise right before the opening { corrupted the frame format. The fix is three lines. But the order matters more than the lines themselves. You need to capture the real stdout before anything else in the process touches it. Before Logback initializes, before a single coroutine launches — before the JVM has any reason to touch stdout. Then redirect System.out to stderr — so every library that "prints normally" lands somewhere the protocol will never read. Then hand your saved reference to the transport. fun main() = runBlocking { val mcpOutput = System.out      // capture the wire first System.setOut(System.err)       // redirect everything else to stderr val transport = StdioServerTransport( input = System.`in`.asSource().buffered(), output = mcpOutput.asSink().buffered() ) // build server, register tools, createSession(transport) } Flip the order and you save a reference to stderr, not stdout. You protect the stream you poisoned. After this swap, System.out is a controlled lie — any library that logs "normally" ends up on stderr, where the MCP client ignores it for framing. The actual wire is mcpOutput , handed directly to StdioServerTransport . They never cross. The server shell — and why it should stay boring With stdout safe, main has one job: wire the protocol skeleton and stay out of the way. If main knows how to parse a business error, it has already gotten too fat. You construct a Server , declare your capabilities, attach the transport, then hand control to a list of registrars that build the actual tool catalog. Domain logic doesn't belong in this file. val server = Server( serverInfo = Implementation(name = "my-kotlin-mcp", version = "1.0.0"), options = ServerOptions( capabilities = ServerCapabilities( tools = ServerCapabilities.Tools(listChanged = true) ) ) ) registrars.forEach { it.register(server) } ServerCapabilities.Tools is what tells the client you have tools to list. Without it, tools/list gets an empty handshake and the agent stops asking. Each registrar calls server.addTool(...) with a name, description, schema, and a suspend handler. We hide that behind one interface so main stays a loop. interface McpToolsRegistrar { fun register(server: Server) } Android engineers already think this way. The shell is the Activity. Registrars are the use cases. Real logic lives another layer down. The SDK shell just gives you one more place to practice the same discipline you already apply everywhere else. Coroutines Close the Loop Cleanly Because MCP tool handlers are suspend functions running within the SDK’s coroutine scope, you can invoke your existing suspend domain logic directly. excerpt: Fourth in a series, and a direct sequel to Another Way to KMP: Shared Renderers. Continue reading on ProAndroidDev »
content: Kmp Android Software Architecture IOS Kotlin Yet Another Way to KMP: One Pattern, Three Seams Gabor Berenyi 7 min read · 5 days ago -- Listen Share Fourth in a series, and a direct sequel to Another Way to KMP: Shared Renderers . Press enter or click to view image in full size Motoman on iOS The last article ended on a claim: isolate the platform API behind a small interface in commonMain , and everything above it can be written once. That result came from porting a 2012 Objective-C iOS app into shared Kotlin and standing up Android alongside it. Good outcome — but a single data point, and one where I controlled the scope. Greenfield and near-greenfield are soft tests of an architecture, because you can always put the boundary where the code is already convenient. So I did it again, deliberately choosing a project that would stress the parts the first one didn’t. Same architecture, different problem motoman-kmp is a Kotlin Multiplatform port of a 2013 Java game by mammalwong (GPL-3.0, ported with the license intact) — it comes with physics simulation on a fixed timestep , a procedural content generation algorithm , an animation system, and a rendering pipeline. Roughly 8,000 lines of behavior that already worked, written by someone else. The architecture is the same as the previous project’s. But: Previous was porting iOS → Android, this one does the opposite; the architecture worked both ways Previous had native UI on each platform, this one has a shared CMP UI Previous supported gestures only, this one takes device sensors, touch and keyboard inputs Previous had 1 shared module, this one has 3 Previous had 1 common unit test, this one has 101 and a golden-frame regression test Below the shared Kotlin we have three different architectural seams , where the previous project only needed one: Press enter or click to view image in full size Seam 1: the platform interface The graphics façade is the pattern from the last article , unchanged: one interface in commonMain enumerating exactly the calls this application makes, one implementation per platform, every implementation a one-liner. That article covers why it's necessary. This one only needs the number. 34 calls there. About 60 here. The workload went up by a large multiple — a full custom game engine against an ambient visualization — and the interface grew by less than 2×. The tax is sub-linear because an interface only covers the calls you actually make, not the API you’re nominally programming against. The underlying API has hundreds of entry points; a real application uses a few dozen, and that set stops growing long before the feature list does. Sixty one-line delegations per platform, written once. That’s the whole cost of not duplicating 8,000 lines. Seam 2: the hardware sensors interface Here’s where the harder workload demanded something the previous project never needed. An ambient visualization only takes camera input — pan, zoom, roll. A game takes input that drives a simulation , including device tilt. On Android that’s SensorManager and a SensorEventListener ; on iOS it's CMMotionManager and CoreMotion . Completely different APIs, lifecycles, and threading models. The obvious approach — and what the code did first — is to handle it per platform. Android read the accelerometer and mapped it to throttle inside MainActivity . iOS didn't implement it at all and just pinned the throttle to a constant. The same seam pattern collapses this: // commonMain — the entire surface the platform must provide interface HardwareSensors { /** Device pitch in m/s². 0 means flat, positive means tilted forward. */ val devicePitch: Float } One property. MainActivity implements it from SensorManager ; the iOS host implements it from CMMotionManager . Everything above it — deadzone, response curve, throttle ceiling, the boost timer — moves into a single InputController in commonMain . The interface is deliberately tiny, and that’s the design rule: the seam carries dumb data, never live platform objects. No SensorEvent , no CMDeviceMotion , no listener registration. One float, already in physical units. Seam 3: a shared @Composable The third boundary is the one the previous project didn’t have at all. There, the HUD and gesture handling were hosted natively — Android and iOS each had their own. That’s defensible when the UI is two toggles and a camera. It stops being defensible when the UI is a control scheme, and this project produced the clearest evidence for why. Both platforms need the same on-screen controls: a drag-to-steer surface, a boost button, a HUD. They were implemented separately — Compose on Android, hand-written touchesBegan/touchesMoved/touchesEnded in Swift on iOS. They drifted. Of course they did. Steering sensitivity is set by a “full lock” distance — how far you drag for maximum steering. Android used a quarter of the screen width. iOS used a hardcoded 300f . On a phone in landscape, that's roughly a third less sensitive. Two platforms, same game, measurably different handling, and nothing in the codebase that would ever flag it. Neither platform passes it in, so neither platform can set it differently. That’s the general lesson, and the one I’d defend hardest: Duplicated platform logic doesn’t stay duplicated. It drifts. title: Data Classes in Kotlin: Say Goodbye to Boilerplate Code
excerpt: Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. You need classes to represent products, users, orders, and addresses. These classes… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Data Classes in Kotlin: Say Goodbye to Boilerplate Code Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 5 days ago -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. You need classes to represent products, users, orders, and addresses. These classes mainly store data and don’t contain much business logic. In Java, writing such classes meant creating constructors, getters, setters, equals() , hashCode() , toString() , and sometimes even a copy() method. That's a lot of repetitive code for a simple model. Press enter or click to view image in full size Kotlin solves this problem with Data Classes . A single keyword — data —can automatically generate all the common utility functions that developers write repeatedly. In this article, you’ll learn what data classes are, why they’re useful, what Kotlin generates automatically, and how they’re used in real-world Android development. What Is a Data Class? A data class is a class whose primary purpose is to hold data . Instead of focusing on behavior, data classes represent objects such as: User Product Employee Order Student Address These objects mainly store information. Creating a data class is simple. data class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) That’s it. With just one line, Kotlin generates several useful functions automatically. Why Do We Need Data Classes? Consider a regular Kotlin class. class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) Now create two objects. val user1 = User("Alex", 25) val user2 = User("Alex", 25) println(user1 == user2) Output: false Even though both objects contain the same values, they are considered different because regular classes compare object references by default. Now use a data class. data class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) Run the same code. val user1 = User("Alex", 25) val user2 = User("Alex", 25) println(user1 == user2) Output: true Data classes compare the contents of the objects instead of their memory addresses. What Does Kotlin Generate Automatically? When you use the data keyword, Kotlin automatically generates: equals() hashCode() toString() copy() componentN() functions This dramatically reduces boilerplate code. toString() Without a data class: User@7a81197d With a data class: data class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) val user = User("Janhvi", 24) println(user) Output: User(name=Janhvi, age=24) This makes debugging much easier. equals() Data classes compare property values automatically. data class Product( val id: Int, val name: String ) val p1 = Product(1, "Laptop") val p2 = Product(1, "Laptop") println(p1 == p2) Output: true This is especially useful when comparing API responses, Room entities, or UI state objects. hashCode() Whenever equals() is generated, Kotlin also generates a matching hashCode() implementation. This allows data class objects to work correctly inside collections like: HashSet HashMap MutableSet Example: val users = hashSetOf( User("Alex", 25), User("Alex", 25) ) println(users.size) Output: 1 Because both objects are equal, only one is stored. copy() One of the most powerful features of data classes is the copy() function. Imagine you have: data class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) Create an object. val user = User("Alex", 25) Now update only the age. val updatedUser = user.copy(age = 26) Output: User(name=Alex, age=26) The original object remains unchanged. This is one of the reasons data classes work so well with immutable programming. componentN() Functions Data classes automatically support destructuring. data class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) val user = User("Alex", 25) val (name, age) = user println(name) println(age) Output: Alex 25 Kotlin internally generates: component1() component2() These enable destructuring declarations. Data Classes and Immutability Most data classes use val instead of var . data class Product( val id: Int, val name: String, val price: Double ) Immutable objects are: Easier to reason about Thread-safe Less prone to bugs Ideal for Jetpack Compose and StateFlow Whenever possible, prefer immutable data classes. Real-World Android Examples API Response Model data class UserResponse( val id: Int, val name: String, val email: String ) Libraries like Retrofit automatically map JSON into these objects. Room Database Entity data class Product( val id: Int, val title: String, val price: Double ) Each object represents a row in the database. UI State data class LoginUiState( val isLoading: Boolean, val error: String?, val userName: String ) Updating state becomes simple. state = state.copy( isLoading = true ) This pattern is widely used in Jetpack Compose and MVI architecture. Shopping Cart data class CartItem( val productId: Int, val quantity: Int ) Need to increase quantity? val updatedItem = cartItem.copy( quantity = cartItem.quantity + 1 ) No mutation required. Requirements for a Data Class A data class must follow a few rules: It must have at least one parameter in the primary constructor. Every primary constructor parameter must be marked with val or var . It cannot be abstract , sealed , open , or inner . Valid: data class Student( val name: String ) Invalid: data class Student() This causes a compilation error because there are no constructor properties. Data Class vs Regular Class Press enter or click to view image in full size Best Practices When working with data classes: Use them for model objects that primarily store data. Prefer val for immutable properties. Use copy() instead of mutating existing objects. Avoid placing complex business logic inside data classes. Keep data classes focused on representing data, not behavior. Use descriptive property names for better readability. These practices make your code easier to test, maintain, and reason about. Interview Tip A common interview question is: Can a data class inherit from another class? Answer: A data class cannot be open or abstract , but it can extend another class or implement int

excerpt: TL;DR KotlinLLM is now public. It’s a research prototype for delegating runtime logic to an LLM from Kotlin code. content:
JetBrains Research Research is crucial for progress and innovation, which is why at JetBrains we are passionate about both scientific and market research About JetBrains Research All News Articles DevEco Kotlin Research KotlinLLM is Going Open Source Anastasia Birillo Stanislav Sandler TL;DR KotlinLLM is now public . It’s a research prototype for delegating runtime logic to an LLM from Kotlin code. Instead of calling an LLM on every request or running a separate agent, you can write an explicit Kotlin call. Its body is generated Kotlin source code , and that code is updated as your application hits new runtime scenarios. 👉 Check it out 👉 KotlinConf 2026 talk What is KotlinLLM? KotlinLLM is an IntelliJ IDEA plugin for Kotlin/JVM projects. It adds a language feature we call Smart macros . A Smart macro is a regular Kotlin function call whose body is generated Kotlin code. The public API has the following two Smart macros: asLlm<F, T>(from, hint) converts an input of type F into a typed value T (data class, enum, list, or primitive). Use it to parse unstructured or semi-structured data into typed Kotlin values at runtime. mockLlm<T>() generates a stateful implementation of an interface T. Its behavior depends on which methods are called on it, so it works as a test double that you don’t have to write by hand. // One level of abstraction higher: describe intent, let KotlinLLM fill in the logic.
val issuesApiUrl: String = asLlm(repoInput, hint = "GitHub API URL: get all issues, including closed")
val issues: List<Issue> = asLlm(response, hint = "Return all beginner-friendly issues for this repository") The behavior comes from actual runtime usage rather than being fully specified before the program runs. The call site stays compact and explicit: a clear, keyword-like API over generated code. The problem it solves In software engineering, LLMs are during development , i.e. code completion, code generation, and program comprehension. Using an LLM at the runtime of a compiled application is less common, and the existing options have clear trade-offs: Direct runtime delegation (calling the model on every invocation) is slow, non-deterministic, and costly. It also makes the application depend on an LLM service at runtime. External agent workflows keep the generated logic outside the codebase, where it’s harder to review, test, and ship. Most prior work (e.g. byLLM , nightjar , Healer ) targets interpreted languages like Python, not a compiled, statically typed language like Kotlin. KotlinLLM is built around three properties: Explicit – the call site shows that a feature is LLM-backed, so it’s visible in code review. Persistent – generated behavior is saved as an ordinary Kotlin source, not kept only in the runtime session. It can be committed, reviewed, tested, and distributed like any other code. Portable – once generated, the code runs as plain Kotlin without the plugin. For scenarios that are already covered, there’s no further LLM call, so no added latency or cost, and the result is reproducible. Does it actually work? We tested the approach on two Kotlin/JVM projects: An adapted Spring Petclinic Kotlin – 18 asLlm call sites, 24/24 application scenarios completed after Smart macro evolution, with a 100% hot-reload success rate and compilation/redefinition adding ~1% of total runtime overhead. A synthetic “GitHub Beginner Issue Radar” – parsing real GitHub issue data across 20 repositories (30k+ issues), reaching ~0.89 recall on ground-truth beginner labels. These results show that persistent runtime evolution for compiled Kotlin is feasible. The evaluation also documents the current limits. We’re making it public KotlinLLM is open source under the Apache License 2.0 . The repository contains: The IntelliJ plugin prototype and the stable Smart macro API. Runnable example projects (GitHub Issue Radar, an adapted Petclinic), including committed generated sources, so you can inspect what the LLM produced and run it as ordinary Kotlin. The KotlinConf2026 talk recording and the theoretical write-up with the full design rationale and evaluation. Try it and tell us what you think KotlinLLM is a research prototype , so feedback is useful at this stage. A few ways to help: Start and explore the repo Try it on your own Kotlin/JVM project . Add the KotlinLLM.kt API file, launch with the Run with KotlinLLM executor, and let the Smart macros evolve. Setup steps are in the README. Open issues for anything you run into: rough edges, unexpected LLM behavior, missing cases, or behavior you’d expect to be different. Send PRs with use cases. Real scenarios where asLlm/mockLlm work well – or break – are the most useful. New examples, target types, and agent tools are all welcome. If you find a place where runtime logic delegation fits your code, open an issue. If you build something with it, send a PR. title: Sealed Classes in Kotlin: Build Safer and More Predictable Applications
excerpt: Imagine you’re building a login screen. After the user taps the Login button, only a few outcomes are possible: the request is loading… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Sealed Classes in Kotlin: Build Safer and More Predictable Applications Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 5 days ago -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building a login screen. After the user taps the Login button, only a few outcomes are possible: the request is loading, the login succeeds, or an error occurs. There shouldn’t be any unexpected state outside of these possibilities. Press enter or click to view image in full size How do you represent these limited states in code? Many beginners use integers, strings, or enums. While these approaches work for simple scenarios, they become difficult to maintain as applications grow. Kotlin introduces Sealed Classes , a powerful language feature that lets you model a fixed set of possible states in a type-safe way. In this article, you’ll learn what sealed classes are, why they’re useful, how they differ from enums, and how they’re used in real Android applications. What Is a Sealed Class? A sealed class represents a restricted hierarchy of classes . Only a predefined set of subclasses can extend a sealed class. For example: Result │ ├── Success ├── Error └── Loading No other class outside this hierarchy can extend Result . This restriction allows the compiler to know every possible type , making your code safer and easier to maintain. Why Do We Need Sealed Classes? Imagine a login screen. Without sealed classes, you might write: var state = "loading" Later: state = "success" Or perhaps: state = "completed" Oops! Nothing prevents someone from assigning an invalid value. Instead, define the allowed states explicitly. sealed class LoginState Now the application can only use the states you define. Creating Your First Sealed Class sealed class LoginState { object Loading : LoginState() object Success : LoginState() data class Error( val message: String ) : LoginState() } Notice something interesting: A sealed class can have different kinds of subclasses: object data class Regular class Each one represents a different state. Understanding the Subclasses Loading object Loading : LoginState() No additional data is required. There can only ever be one loading state. Success object Success : LoginState() Again, no additional information is needed. Error data class Error( val message: String ) : LoginState() Errors usually need extra information, such as an error message. That’s why a data class is used. Using a Sealed Class fun handleState( state: LoginState ) { when(state) { is LoginState.Loading -> println("Loading...") is LoginState.Success -> println("Login Successful") is LoginState.Error -> println(state.message) } } Notice that no else branch is required . Why? Because Kotlin already knows every possible subclass. This is called an exhaustive when expression . It’s one of the biggest advantages of sealed classes. Exhaustive when Suppose you later add another state. object LoggedOut : LoginState() Now your existing when statement won't compile until you handle the new state. This prevents bugs caused by forgotten cases. Sealed Classes with Data Subclasses can contain different information. sealed class PaymentResult { data class Success( val transactionId: String ) : PaymentResult() data class Failure( val reason: String ) : PaymentResult() object Processing : PaymentResult() } Usage: val result = PaymentResult.Success( "TXN12345" ) Each state carries only the data it actually needs. Sealed Class vs Enum Many beginners wonder: Should I use an enum or a sealed class? Let’s compare them. Press enter or click to view image in full size Example enum: enum class OrderStatus { PENDING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED } Useful when values don’t need additional information. But if each state needs different data, use a sealed class. Real-World Android Example: UI State One of the most common Android use cases. sealed class UiState { object Loading : UiState() data class Success( val users: List<String> ) : UiState() data class Error( val message: String ) : UiState() } ViewModel: var state: UiState = UiState.Loading Compose UI: when (state) { is UiState.Loading -> { // Show ProgressBar } is UiState.Success -> { // Show Data } is UiState.Error -> { // Show Error } } This pattern is widely used in Jetpack Compose , MVVM , and MVI architectures. API Response Example Instead of returning null , create a sealed result. sealed class ApiResult<T> { data class Success<T>( val data: T ) : ApiResult<T>() data class Error<T>( val message: String ) : ApiResult<T>() class Loading<T> : ApiResult<T>() } Repository: fun fetchUsers(): ApiResult<List<User>> The caller now knows exactly what outcomes are possible. Error Handling sealed class NetworkError { object NoInternet : NetworkError() object Timeout : NetworkError() data class ServerError( val code: Int ) : NetworkError() } Instead of checking integers like: if(code == 404) You work with meaningful types. Navigation Example sealed class Screen { object Home : Screen() object Profile : Screen() data class Details( val productId: Int ) : Screen() } Usage: navigate( Screen.Details(101) ) Each destination carries only the arguments it needs. Sealed Interface Kotlin also supports sealed interfaces . sealed interface DownloadState They provide the same restricted hierarchy while allowing greater flexibility with inheritance. Use them when multiple unrelated class hierarchies need to share the same contract. Best Practices When using sealed classes: Use them to model a fixed number of states. Prefer object for states without data. Use data class for states that carry information. Keep the hierarchy small and focused. Take advantage of exhaustive when expressions. Use sealed classes for UI state, API results, navigation, and error handling. These practices make your applications safer and easier to maintain. content: Press enter or click to view image in full size Banglish Keyboard & Converter Android Kotlin Python AI Open Source I Built an AI-Powered Banglish Keyboard That Converts Text Instantly — Here’s How Rafiul islam 7 min read · 4 days ago -- Listen Share From a simple idea to a dual-platform tool powered by Groq AI By Rafiul Islam — IoT & Robotics Engineer The Problem Every Bangladeshi Faces If you’re Bangladeshi, you know exactly what Banglish is — even if you’ve never heard the word. It’s how we type every single day: “ami aj office theke fire khub tired, ektu rest nibo. kal meeting ache, presentation ready korte hobe raat er moddhe” Bengali words written in English script, mixed with actual English words — that’s Banglish. We do it on WhatsApp, Messenger, Facebook, everywhere. The problem? When you actually need proper বাংলা Unicode text — for formal writing, social media captions, or sending to someone who can’t read Banglish — you have to manually retype everything. Or use a translator that doesn’t understand our informal mixed language at all. Google Translate fails at Banglish. Avro keyboard helps with typing বাংলা but doesn’t convert existing Banglish text. Nothing solved this specific problem. So I built a tool that does exactly that. Press enter or click to view image in full size What I Built AI Banglish Keyboard is a dual-platform tool — a Windows desktop app and an Android app — that converts Banglish text to proper বাংলা Unicode or clean English, powered by Groq AI. Desktop version: Runs silently in the system tray Press Ctrl+Shift+B → any Banglish text in any app converts to বাংলা Press Ctrl+Shift+E → converts to English Works in WhatsApp Web, Chrome, Notepad, VS Code — literally anywhere Android version: Standalone converter app Type Banglish → tap a button → instant conversion Copy or share directly to WhatsApp, Messenger, anywhere Press enter or click to view image in full size Keyboard Workflow Why Groq AI? I initially planned to use the Anthropic Claude API, but it requires a paid subscription. Then I discovered Groq — a free AI inference platform that offers blazing fast response times and a generous free tier. Groq free tier limits: 30 requests/minute 14,400 requests/day Cost: $0 forever The model I chose: llama-3.3-70b-versatile — one of the best open-source LLMs available, running on Groq's custom LPU hardware for incredibly fast inference. The key insight was that this isn’t a simple translation task. Banglish conversion requires: Transliteration — Roman script → Bengali script Semantic understanding — understanding informal language and slang Context preservation — keeping the tone, emotion, and meaning intact Rule-based systems fail at this. LLMs excel at it. The System Prompt — Most Important Part The quality of conversion depends entirely on how well you instruct the AI. Here’s the system prompt I crafted after multiple iterations: You are a specialized Banglish text converter for Bangladeshi users. DEFINITION: Banglish = Bengali language written in English/Roman script, mixed with actual English words. This is exactly how Bangladeshis type in social media, WhatsApp, Messenger, etc. STRICT RULES: 1. Preserve original meaning, tone, and emotion exactly 2. Handle informal language, slang, and code-mixing naturally 3. For বাংলা target: Use proper Unicode Bengali script only 4. For English target: Write natural, grammatically correct English 5. Return ONLY the converted text — zero explanations, zero extra text Example input: “bhai ki korcho, urgent call daw ektu, onek important kotha ache” → বাংলা output: “ভাই কী করছ, একটু আর্জেন্ট কল দাও, অনেক গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কথা আছে” → English output: “Bro what are you doing, give me an urgent call, I have something very important to discuss” The LLM handles slang, informal contractions, and mixed language naturally — something no rule-based system could do. WhatsApp Web shows unknown device? You are not paranoid. Here is what I found after testing 20+ phones. WhatsApp says it's end-to-end encrypted. That's true. But your phone is not. After running Halol Droid blog for 3 years and helping 500k+ Android users, I see the same 5 signs every time someone's WhatsApp is compromised. 1. Battery drains 30% faster Spyware runs in background 24/7. If your battery drops from 100% to 70% in 2 hours without use, check Settings > Battery > WhatsApp usage. 2. WhatsApp Web shows a device you don't recognize Open WhatsApp > Linked Devices. If you see "Windows - Chrome" and you never linked it, someone is reading your chats LIVE. Remove it immediately. 3. Your messages are marked as "read" before you open them Two blue ticks while your phone is locked = someone else opened it on Web. 4. Phone gets hot when idle No game, no video, but phone is hot? Background recorder is active. 5. You hear strange noises in calls Clicking, echo, or voice delay. Classic call forwarding trick. How to fix it in 30 seconds: 1. Go to Linked Devices > Log out from all devices 2. Enable Two-Step Verification: Settings > Privacy > Two-step 3. Update WhatsApp from Play Store (many old versions have Web bug) 4. Kotlin A concise multiplatform language developed by JetBrains Follow Follow: X X RSS RSS Visit the Kotlin Site Backend News Tutorials Secure Your APIs: OAuth2 and JWT for Beginners Alina Dolgikh This tutorial was written by an external contributor. Mdu Sibisi Mdu Sibisi is an Oracle-certified software developer and blogger with over ten years of experience working primarily with object-oriented languages. He has been writing about technology for more than eight years, focusing on making complex topics easier to understand. Mdu is passionate about accessible developer education, clean code, and creating content that helps developers learn and grow. Website | Twitter Repository with the companion code for the tutorial Go to GitHub APIs are frequent targets for bad actors since they expose data and functionality. Securing them while maintaining usability is often one of the most challenging and time-consuming parts of API development. OAuth 2.0 and JSON Web Tokens (JWT) help make these processes more manageable and reliable. They allow developers to represent and verify identity and manage access by safely transmitting claims and enabling delegated authorization. This article discusses these technologies and the most efficient ways you can use them to secure your Spring Boot-built APIs and backends. If you’re interested in a coroutine‑driven solution, a companion tutorial using Ktor is also planned and will be published soon. OAuth2 and JWT Primer OAuth2 and JWT(s) aren’t competing technologies. They’re complementary pieces of the puzzle, with one handling the delegation of authorization and the other serving as the compact, verifiable token format that carries secure information. Authentication vs. Authorization Authentication verifies identity (who you are), usually through credentials like passwords, tokens, or certificates. JWTs can carry identity information and act like a form of ID once issued. Roles and other claims within a JWT are then used for authorization. Authorization helps control what a user has access to (what they can do). This includes the scopes or resources that they can “touch” and how those permissions are managed. In a system that uses OAuth2 and JWT, the access badge is bundled into your ID card. OAuth2 oversees and manages this process. The Role of OAuth2 OAuth2 is a framework for delegated access. Instead of sharing passwords directly, users grant applications a token that represents their permissions. This means that your backend (acting as a Resource Server ) doesn’t have to issue tokens. Instead, it trusts and validates the ones coming from the Authorization Server within OAuth2’s framework. This decoupling of duties allows you to simplify your APIs while reducing security risks and ensuring all tokens follow a clear, consistent, centralized policy. You don’t have to worry about implementing user logins or browser redirects within your API. As far as validation and authorization are concerned, your backend or API’s job is to receive the Bearer Token , authenticate the signature, check expiration, and enforce scopes/roles. Your API just checks badges; it’s not responsible for printing them. So how do JWTs fit into the equation? What Is a JWT? A JWT is a small, web-friendly piece of text (string) that securely transports information between systems. Their compactness makes them easy to pass around in HTTP headers or URLs. Each token uses Base64URL encoding , making them safe to include in query strings or headers. JWTs are signed (and sometimes encrypted), so that recipients can verify that they weren’t tampered with. They’re also self-contained, carrying details like user ID, roles, or permissions. These elements (especially self-containment and signing) allow for stateless authentication without Session Storage . This means that you don’t need a database or cache to track active sessions. It also encourages fewer lookups and less infrastructure complexity, which reduces your system’s overhead. JWTs have a very simple, standardized structure made up of three parts, separated by dots: The Header contains metadata about the token, such as the type ( JWT ) and the signing algorithm ( HS256 , RS256 ). The Payload features the claims, which are statements about the user or system (like user ID, roles, or token expiry). The Signature is a cryptographic signature created using the header, payload, and a secret or private key. This ensures the token has not been tampered with. The basic structure of a JWT looks like this: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz A real-world Base64URL-encoded token typically resembles the following: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ
.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c When OAuth2 meets JWT There are four key roles in OAuth2’s implementation: Resource Owner: The entity (usually the user) granting access to the protected resources. Client: The application requesting access to the resource on behalf of the resource owner. Authorization Server: The server that authenticates the resource owner and issues access tokens to the client. Resource Server: The server hosting the protected resources, which accepts and validates tokens. The Resource Owner grants permission ( e.g. , you click “Allow” when an app requests access), the Client then requests authorization from the Authorization Server, which issues an access token (JWT) if the Resource Owner approves. The Client uses this access token to access data from the Resource Server. Note: It’s important to note that JWTs aren’t the only token format that OAuth2 can work with; it’s just the most popular because of its perks. OAuth2 can also work with Opaque Tokens , SAML Tokens , or custom token formats like Microsoft’s reference tokens or Google’s access tokens.           developers. 🔍 Android Developers → Jetpack Kotlin Docs News Platform Android Studio Google Play Jetpack Kotlin Docs News Platform Android Studio Google Play Jetpack Kotlin Docs News More | 29 July 2026 Delivering safer, age-appropriate experiences on Google Play Share this post LinkedIn Twitter Facebook Email Copy link Link copied to clipboard Posted by Paul Feng, VP of Product Management, Google Play Providing a safe online experience and protecting users from harm is a top priority at Google Play. We take this responsibility seriously and have been investing continuously to offer baseline protections on our platform while also empowering parents with the tools they need to make decisions for their families. Importantly, we also want to empower Play developers with the capabilities to deliver age-appropriate experiences based on their app's content. To support this, today, we are taking another big step in our ongoing partnership with parents and developers by announcing the expansion of the Google Play Age Signals API to all Play developers globally. Building on current availability in Brazil, we will expand this experience first to users in Australia and Canada by mid-August, with a full global rollout to all users later this year. Empowering developers to create age-appropriate experiences The Play Age Signals API is a privacy-preserving tool that puts parents in the driver's seat allowing them to share their child's age range (e.g. 16-17) directly with apps. It also enables adults to easily share their age when prompted by the app developer. In turn, developers receive the signals they need to tailor their own in-app safety experiences and content for users in an age-appropriate way. We want to give developers the ability to choose the right protections for the nature of their app. A weather app, for example, shouldn't need the same safety settings as entertainment or media apps. Rather than enforcing one-size-fits-all rules, we give developers the flexibility to choose how they integrate safety signals. With this reliable signal, you retain complete agency to tailor your app's content, features, and settings to match your audience. Users have a choice to share their age range in a privacy-friendly way Simplifying controls for parents Parents shouldn't have to manage complex safety settings across dozens of different apps to keep their children safe. The Play Age Signals API simplifies this by putting age-sharing controls in one place, directly inside the Google Family Link app . Parents have a choice to share their child’s age range, and if they choose to share, all Play apps that use Play Age Signals API can receive age signals. This lets children jump straight into age-appropriate content without parents having to manually configure settings inside these apps. Age ranges are never shared by default, and parents can update or turn off these settings at any time. Centralized and easy way to manage age sharing settings for parents via Family Link App Building on our broader safety tools The Play Age Signals API builds upon a strong foundation of established safety features and strict policies we have long enforced on Google Play. Today, we already mandate that apps designed for families meet rigorous safety standards , and we continuously review and scan applications to ensure they are safe for children. For developers, we also offer built-in tools like Restrict Minor Access in the Play Console to help them manage who can discover their apps. For parents, Google Family Link remains a trusted, central dashboard where they can manage screen-time limits, PIN-based content filters , and app download approvals. Expanding the Play Age Signals API globally adds a powerful new tool to our existing safety suite, helping parents and developers work together to make Google Play an even safer, more trustworthy place for families. content: Qodana The code quality platform for teams Follow Follow: X X RSS RSS Get Qodana All News Tutorials Features Opinion Qodana 2026.2: More Security, Better Coverage, Less Configuration Kerry Beetge Qodana 2026.2 makes it easier for development teams to act on code quality, security, and compliance findings throughout the development workflow. This release introduces clearer code coverage insights for pull requests, highlights uncovered new lines directly in the IDE, and automatically detects coverage reports in common project locations – reducing the configuration required to get started. The release also expands Qodana’s security offering with new inspections, support for custom security rules, post-quantum cryptography inspections, and publicly available SAST benchmarks through SABER. Laravel inspections are now enabled by default, while new License Audit quality gates help teams prevent newly introduced dependencies with prohibited or unknown licences from progressing through the pipeline. Let’s get into the details. Try Qodana Better Code Coverage UX Code Coverage for incremental analysis in the IDE Starting with Qodana 2026.2, pull request analyses can show which changed or added lines are covered by tests and which are not, alongside the total coverage for newly added code, known as fresh coverage. After the analysis, developers can open the report in the IDE and browse the files changed in the pull request. They can see which files lack coverage through statistics in the tool window, while new lines are highlighted in the IDE to reveal coverage gaps. Developers can use this information to write targeted tests for functionality that lacks coverage, improving the reliability of their software. Out-of-the-box code coverage reporting Showing code coverage results in Qodana now requires fewer configuration steps. You no longer need to copy all reports to the .qodana/code-coverage directory, which lets you simplify your build configuration. Qodana 2026.2 automatically detects coverage reports in the project: Qodana for JVM and Qodana for Android: default paths for Jacoco and Kover plugins are supported for both Maven and Gradle Qodana for JS: default location coverage/lcov.info is supported, as well as some common community locations like reports or test-coverage directories Qodana for PHP: clover.xml and coverage.xml files are supported in common in community locations, such as the project root, build/logs , reports and coverage Qodana for Python: coverage.xml file is supported in common locations like project root, coverage-reports or reports Qodana for Go: coverage.out or cover.out files in root directory and other common directories like coverage , reports are supported Qodana for .NET: coverage.cobertura and coverage.info files in project root or other common directories like coverage or TestResults are supported To generate code coverage reports, set up one of the supported tools , and see your statistics in any run. To disable this behaviour, either selectively copy your reports to the .qodana/code-coverage directory , or specify your custom location using a new codeCoverageLocations parameter in your qodana.yaml file. See the documentation for an example of how to specify a custom directory. To disable coverage reporting, disable the corresponding inspection in your configuration. View Documentation New security inspections Broader SAST and multi-file taint analysis Qodana 2026.2 expands the security analysis available in the Qodana for .NET linter, helping teams detect a broader range of vulnerabilities in C#, JavaScript, and TypeScript code. The new inspections are enabled by default in the recommended profile and appear as standard Qodana findings within existing IDE, CI/CD, and reporting workflows. The expanded inspection set combines two forms of analysis. Pattern-matching rules identify insecure coding practices within individual code locations, while taint analysis tracks untrusted data as it moves through an application, including across multiple files. This enables Qodana to detect vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, command injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and path traversal. Teams can also extend this coverage with their own security rules. Qodana for .NET now supports custom and third-party rules written in the OpenGrep format. Place these rules in the .qodana/opengrep directory at the project root, and Qodana will make them available as Qodana inspections. The predefined rules are publicly available in the opengrep-sast-rules repository. Behind the scenes, pattern matching uses an open-source JetBrains fork of OpenGrep, while data-flow tracking is handled by Qodana’s own taint analysis engine. This gives teams access to the OpenGrep rule format and ecosystem while retaining Qodana’s multi-file analysis and developer workflows. Support will be extended to additional Qodana linters and languages (Kotlin/Java) in future releases.
