title: From Object to Any — Why Kotlin Replaced Java’s Base Class
excerpt: How platform independence, null safety, and JVM interop shaped Kotlin’s class hierarchy Continue reading on Level Up Coding »
content: Kotlin Android Java Android App Development Programming From Object to Any — Why Kotlin Replaced Java’s Base Class How platform independence, null safety, and JVM interop shaped Kotlin’s class hierarchy Dilipchandar 4 min read · 3 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size When Java was the primary programming language to develop Android Apps, we would have noticed the Object class from java.lang.Object package. And we might have encountered the famous interview question Q: What is the base class of Java? A: Object And maybe the follow-up question, Q: What are the methods of the Object class? A: wait(), notify(), notifyAll(), clone(), toString(), hashCode(), finalize(), getClass(), equals() Press enter or click to view image in full size We can see from the above screenshot that the Object class of the java.lang package exists for Java, and an important point to note is that the Object class is the root of the class hierarchy. Most Kotlin developers use Any which is the base class of Kotlin every day without realising it replaced an entire Java class — and the reasons why reveal a lot about how Kotlin was designed. Why did Kotlin replace the Object class? In Kotlin, there is no class named Object because it is replaced by Any , which serves as the root of the entire Kotlin class hierarchy. Every Kotlin class implicitly inherits from Any . Kotlin deliberately chose to introduce Any instead of reusing Java's java.lang.Object for several architectural and design reasons. Platform Independence Kotlin is designed to be a multiplatform language . It does not just run on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM); it also compiles to JavaScript (Kotlin/JS) and native machine code (Kotlin/Native for iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux) . Reusing a Java-specific class like java.lang.Object as the universal base class would tie Kotlin permanently to the JVM ecosystem. By using Any , Kotlin maintains a platform-agnostic abstraction that can cleanly map to whatever root structure the target platform uses. Cleaner Universal Abstraction Java’s Object contains low-level, JVM-specific threading methods like wait() , notify() , and notifyAll() . These methods do not make sense on platforms like JavaScript or iOS native environments. Any exposes only the three core methods required for basic object mechanics across any platform: equals() , hashCode() , and toString() . The screenshot below confirms this. Press enter or click to view image in full size Null Safety Integration Get Dilipchandar ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Kotlin is built from the ground up around strict null safety. In Java, a Object reference can always be null . In Kotlin, Any represents a strictly non-nullable value. If you want a variable that can hold absolutely any value including null, you must explicitly use its nullable counterpart, Any? . Mapping Under the Hood Even though you write Any in your Kotlin code, the Kotlin compiler is highly optimized for performance: When compiling for the JVM , the compiler automatically maps Any directly to java.lang.Object in the bytecode. This design choice ensures 100% interoperability with Java libraries without incurring any runtime memory or performance overhead. So how do we create an object of type Object in Kotlin? Either through a constructor class DummyKotlinClass { val obj = Object() fun start() { obj.notify() obj.`class` obj.wait() obj.notifyAll() obj.hashCode() } } or getter class DummyKotlinClass { val obj: Object get() { return obj } fun start() { obj.notify() obj.`class` obj.wait() obj.notifyAll() obj.hashCode() } } Now the methods that are omitted by Kotlin's Any are accessible. One method that is deprecated and not accessible I am talking about the finalize() method of the Object class, which is deprecated since Java 9 and not accessible in Java / Kotlin file from Android Studio. Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size The finalize() method is declared as protected in the java.lang.Object class to allow subclasses to override it for custom cleanup while preventing external classes from invoking it maliciously or accidentally. Why was it deprecated? The garbage collection (GC) mechanism was never intended to reliably manage non-memory resources. Relying on finalize() introduces major flaws: No Time Guarantees : There is no guarantee when or if the garbage collector will run , meaning resources like file streams or database connections can remain open indefinitely. Performance Hangups : Objects with overridden finalize() methods require extra tracking and multiple GC cycles to destroy fully, dragging down application performance. Security Flaws : A failing finalize() method can accidentally "resurrect" a dead object by linking it back to a live reference, creating memory leaks and security bugs. Key Takeaway for Android Devs Any isn't just a renamed Object — it's a deliberate architectural decision that makes Kotlin platform-agnostic, null-safe, and cleaner by design, while remaining fully interoperable with Java under the hood. Understanding these things will help us maintain legacy codebases in Java that are still not yet migrated to Kotlin. Hope this article is a good read. Thanks for reading this article. title: Enum Classes in Kotlin: A Complete Guide with Real-World Examples
excerpt: Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. Every order can only be in one of a few predefined states: Pending, Processing, Shipped… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Enum Classes in Kotlin: A Complete Guide with Real-World Examples Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 3 days ago -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building an e-commerce application. Every order can only be in one of a few predefined states: Pending , Processing , Shipped , Delivered , or Cancelled . It wouldn’t make sense for an order status to suddenly become "Flying" or "Unknown" . Press enter or click to view image in full size One approach is to use strings. var status = "Pending" But what happens if someone accidentally writes: status = "Pendding" The compiler won’t stop you. This is where Enum Classes come in. Enums allow you to define a fixed set of constant values , making your code safer, more readable, and easier to maintain. In this article, you’ll learn everything about Kotlin enum classes, including their syntax, properties, functions, best practices, real-world Android examples, and how they compare with sealed classes. What Is an Enum Class? An enum class is a special type of class used to represent a fixed set of constant values . Think of it as a list of predefined options. For example: Days of the week Order status Payment type User role Theme mode Priority level Instead of allowing any value, an enum restricts the possible values to a known set. Creating Your First Enum enum class Direction { NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST } Now create a variable. val direction = Direction.NORTH println(direction) Output: NORTH Only the four defined values are allowed. Trying to assign anything else results in a compilation error. Why Use Enum Classes? Suppose you represent order status using strings. var status = "Delivered" Later someone writes: status = "Delievered" Notice the spelling mistake. The compiler accepts it, but your application now contains invalid data. With an enum: enum class OrderStatus { PENDING, PROCESSING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED } Only valid values can be assigned. val status = OrderStatus.DELIVERED Enums provide type safety and eliminate many common bugs caused by invalid strings. Accessing Enum Values Assign a value. val status = OrderStatus.SHIPPED Compare values. if (status == OrderStatus.SHIPPED) { println("Order is on the way.") } Output: Order is on the way. Enums are commonly used inside when expressions. Using when with Enums when (status) { OrderStatus.PENDING -> println("Waiting") OrderStatus.PROCESSING -> println("Preparing") OrderStatus.SHIPPED -> println("On the way") OrderStatus.DELIVERED -> println("Completed") } Since Kotlin knows all possible enum values, the compiler can verify that every case is handled. Enum Properties Enums can store additional information. enum class Priority( val level: Int ) { LOW(1), MEDIUM(2), HIGH(3) } Usage: println(Priority.HIGH.level) Output: 3 This is useful when each constant has associated metadata. Enum Functions Enums can also contain member functions. enum class PaymentMethod { CARD, UPI, CASH; fun display() { println("Selected: $name") } } Usage: PaymentMethod.UPI.display() Output: Selected: UPI Notice the semicolon ( ; ) before the function. It's required when adding properties or functions after the enum constants. Overriding Functions for Individual Constants Each enum constant can provide its own implementation. enum class Operation { ADD { override fun apply(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b }, SUBTRACT { override fun apply(a: Int, b: Int) = a - b }; abstract fun apply(a: Int, b: Int): Int } Usage: println(Operation.ADD.apply(10, 5)) println(Operation.SUBTRACT.apply(10, 5)) Output: 15 5 This pattern is useful when each constant behaves differently. Built-in Enum Properties Every enum automatically provides two useful properties. name Returns the constant’s name. println(OrderStatus.SHIPPED.name) Output: SHIPPED ordinal Returns the constant’s position. println(OrderStatus.SHIPPED.ordinal) Output: 2 Since counting starts from zero: PENDING     -> 0 PROCESSING  -> 1 SHIPPED     -> 2 DELIVERED   -> 3 ⚠️ Avoid using ordinal for business logic. If you later reorder the constants, the values change and can introduce subtle bugs. Iterating Through Enum Values You can access every enum constant. for (status in OrderStatus.entries) { println(status) } Output: PENDING PROCESSING SHIPPED DELIVERED Note: entries is available in Kotlin 1.9+. In older versions, use values() . Converting Strings to Enums Sometimes API responses return strings. val status = OrderStatus.valueOf("SHIPPED") println(status) Output: SHIPPED If the string doesn’t match any enum constant exactly, valueOf() throws an exception. For safer parsing, consider wrapping it in runCatching {} or using a custom lookup function. Real-World Android Examples Theme Selection enum class ThemeMode { LIGHT, DARK, SYSTEM } The application can switch themes based on the selected value. User Roles enum class UserRole { ADMIN, SELLER, CUSTOMER } Permissions can be granted based on the user’s role. Network Status enum class NetworkStatus { CONNECTED, DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING } The UI can display different screens depending on the connection state. Notification Priority enum class NotificationPriority { LOW, NORMAL, HIGH } The application can adjust notification behavior using these predefined priorities. Enum vs Sealed Class A common question is: Should I use an enum or a sealed class? Press enter or click to view image in full size Use an Enum When: Representing fixed constants. No additional data is needed. All values share similar behavior. Examples: Days Months User roles Priority Theme mode Use a Sealed Class When: States carry different data. Each state has unique behavior. You’re modelling UI state or API responses. Example: sealed class LoginState { object Loading : LoginState() data class Success( val userName: String ) : LoginState() data class Error( val message: String ) : LoginState() } Best Practices When using enum classes: Use enums for fixed sets of constants. title: Be kind, because you don’t know what they’re going through
excerpt: Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android Life Health Family Be kind, because you don’t know what they’re going through zianmre 2 min read · 3 days ago -- Share Press enter or click to view image in full size pict from Pinterest Ada pepatah yang pernah kudengar, bunyinya kira-kira seperti ini “Jika tidak bisa jadi orang baik, jangan jadi orang jahat.” Hanya sepuluh kata itu, namun mampu membawaku kembali pada ingatan di sekolah dulu. Kala itu, setiap jam istirahat ataupun jam pulang, aku selalu memperhatikan apa yang sedang dilakukan oleh seorang bapak paruh baya. Rupanya, beliau sedang menyapu bersih lingkungan sekolah agar kami—murid-murid di sana—bisa belajar dengan nyaman. Pagi-pagi sekali bapak itu sudah datang, demi memastikan setiap sudut tempat menimba ilmu itu selalu bersih. Suatu hari di jam istirahat, saat aku duduk di bangku kayu sambil menyantap siomay, atensiku seketika teralih ke arah keriuhan. Bapak yang selalu menyapu sampah-sampah yang dibuang sembarangan itu... kini dilempari plastik bekas makanan. Mereka, anak-anak itu—tertawa sambil melempar sampah tepat ke hadapannya, tak peduli jika sisa-sisa makanan mengotori pakaiannya. Namun bukannya marah, bapak itu justru tersenyum sambil memunguti remah-remah sampah yang berserakan. Lalu saat pulang sekolah, di sudut lampu merah, aku melihat seseorang yang membaluri tubuhnya dengan cat perak. Ia berjalan ke sana kemari hanya demi bertahan hidup satu hari lagi. Tak peduli teriknya matahari berpadu dengan cat yang bisa saja membuat kulitnya melepuh. Aku juga melihat seseorang yang mengenakan kostum kartun lucu, menari-nari di samping kendaraan yang berhenti, lalu berpindah ke kendaraan lainnya. Tak bisa kubayangkan betapa panas dan beratnya kostum itu. Tak jauh dari sana, ada pula penjual yang mendorong gerobaknya sambil sesekali mengusap keringat, serta mereka yang hanya menenteng barang dagangannya sambil terus berjalan tak kenal lelah. Laku atau tidak, semuanya tetap mereka syukuri. Sungguh, petang itu benar-benar menyapu lelah dari beragam takdir kehidupan. Mereka masih selalu tersenyum—meski dihina karena pekerjaannya, atau bahkan ditindas. Senyum mereka tak pernah luntur. Hal itu membuatku merenung dan merasa, “Mungkin, aku yang kurang bersyukur.” Aku malu, sungguh malu. Tuhan... aku malu saat mengutuk hari yang kuanggap tak adil padaku—sementara mereka selalu mengumbar senyum saat menghadapi kerasnya cobaan hidup. So, be kind . Jangan samakan satu menit milikmu dengan milik mereka. Bisa jadi, hidup yang sedang kamu keluhkan saat ini adalah kehidupan yang paling mereka impikan. Baju yang malu kamu pakai, butuh perjuangan panjang bagi mereka untuk memilikinya. Makanan yang dimasak ibu di rumah—yang mungkin kamu bosani lauknya—butuh tetesan keringat yang tak sedikit agar mereka bisa menikmati sepiring yang sama. Jika tak bisa jadi orang baik, setidaknya jangan jadi orang jahat. Dan jangan pernah lupa untuk selalu bersyukur.

title: The Hidden Cost of Convenience: What Android Permissions Are Really Tracking
excerpt: Ever wonder what your apps are really tracking? A closer look at Android permissions — and the small habit that quietly takes back control… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full size What your Android permissions are quietly tracking. Privacy Android Technology Self Improvement Mobile Apps The Hidden Cost of Convenience: What Android Permissions Are Really Tracking Amal Amin 4 min read · 3 days ago -- Listen Share A few weeks ago, I was scrolling through my phone’s settings, half-bored, half-curious. I tapped into " App Permissions " just to see what was there. I wasn’t ready for what I found. A flashlight app I installed two years ago and forgot about still had access to my microphone. A photo editor I used exactly once still had permission to read my contacts. A game — a simple, offline puzzle game — somehow had access to my location. None of these apps needed any of that. And I had said yes to all of it, without really reading a single word. That’s the part that stuck with me. I didn’t get tricked by some scam app. I just tapped " Allow " the way we all do, over and over, because a little popup was standing between me and the thing I actually wanted to do. We Trade Privacy for Speed Think about the last time an app asked for permission. Did you read it? Or did you just tap " Allow " so the app would stop bothering you? Most of us do the second one. Not because we don’t care about privacy — but because: We’re in a hurry The popup feels like an obstacle, not a decision We assume the app " probably " needs it Saying no sometimes breaks the app anyway That last one is the real trap. Some apps are built so that if you deny a permission, they just stop working properly. So you give in. Not because you trust the app — but because you want it to function. This is the quiet deal we make with convenience. We don’t hand over our privacy in one big moment. We give it away one small " Allow " at a time, until one day we look back and realize how much access is sitting on our phone. What’s Actually Being Tracked Here’s the part that surprised me most: it’s rarely one big invasion. It’s small, ongoing collection that adds up. Location — not just when you use maps, but sometimes in the background, even when the app is closed Microphone — some apps can technically listen in short bursts, even when you’re not recording anything Contacts — apps that have nothing to do with messaging or calling still request this, often to build a picture of who you know Storage and photos — access to your entire gallery, even if the app only needs one image Usage patterns — how long you use an app, what time of day, how often you open it Why This Matters More Than It Seems easy to think, " I have nothing to hide, so who cares?" But this isn’t really about hiding anything. It’s about who gets to know things about your life without you choosing to tell them. Your location history can reveal where you live, work, and spend your evenings. Your contact list can reveal your relationships. Your app usage patterns can reveal your habits, your mood, even your sleep schedule. None of this is stolen in a dramatic hack. It’s handed over, permission by permission, because we were moving too fast to notice. The Small Shift That Changes Everything I’m not saying delete every app or go live off-grid. That’s not realistic, and honestly, it’s not necessary. What actually helped me was much simpler: I started asking one question before tapping " Allow ." " Does this app actually need this to do its job?" A flashlight app doesn’t need your microphone. A puzzle game doesn’t need your location. A photo editor doesn’t need your contact list. Once I started asking that question, I began saying no more often — and almost nothing broke. Most apps work perfectly fine with fewer permissions than they ask for. They just ask for more because most people never say no. A Quiet Kind of Control There’s something surprisingly calming about going through your permissions and taking a few back. It’s not paranoia. It’s just closing a few doors you never meant to leave open. You don’t need to become a privacy expert overnight. You just need five minutes, a bit of curiosity, and the willingness to tap " Don’t Allow " every once in a while instead of " Allow ." I write about this kind of thing regularly on my blog, Amber Android Brain, where I break down Android settings and problems in plain language — no jargon, just real answers for real phones. But you don’t need my blog to start. You just need to open your settings and look. That’s where it begins — not with fear, but with a little more awareness of what convenience is quietly costing you.

content: Upi Payment Android Development Kotlin Fintechengineering Mobile Payments UPI Payment Flow on Android: From URI Construction to Result Verification Vaibhav Shakya | Mr Neo 4 min read · Jan 9, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size UPI has become the default payment mechanism for Android applications in India. Most Android apps integrate UPI using standard intent-based flows , where payments are executed inside external UPI apps and results are returned back to the calling app. This article explains how to build a robust and modern UPI payment flow on Android using Kotlin , covering: UPI URI construction Triggering UPI apps via intents Receiving and validating responses Handling success, failure, and cancellation states safely The focus is on correct implementation and defensive handling , rather than assumptions. How UPI Payments Work on Android On Android, UPI works through a URI scheme understood by UPI-enabled apps. The flow is simple: Your app constructs a UPI payment URI An external UPI app is launched via an intent The user completes the payment in the UPI app The UPI app returns control to your app Your app receives a response string and interprets it Your application never handles credentials, PINs, or payment execution directly. The UPI URI Format UPI payment requests use the following base scheme: upi://pay Common Parameters ParameterDescription pa Payee Virtual Payment Address pn Payee name am Amount cu Currency (INR) tn Transaction note tr Transaction reference Example upi://pay?pa=test@upi&pn=Test%20Merchant&am=100.00&cu=INR&tr=TXN123 Constructing the UPI URI in Kotlin Always use Uri.Builder to ensure proper encoding. fun buildUpiUri( payeeVpa: String, payeeName: String, amount: String, transactionRef: String, note: String ): Uri { return Uri.Builder() .scheme("upi") .authority("pay") .appendQueryParameter("pa", payeeVpa) .appendQueryParameter("pn", payeeName) .appendQueryParameter("am", amount) .appendQueryParameter("cu", "INR") .appendQueryParameter("tr", transactionRef) .appendQueryParameter("tn", note) .build() } Launching the UPI App (Modern Android API) The legacy onActivityResult() API is deprecated and should not be used. Instead, use Activity Result APIs , which are lifecycle-aware and recommended. private val upiLauncher = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.StartActivityForResult()) { result -> if (result.resultCode == Activity.RESULT_OK) { val response = result.data?.getStringExtra("response") handleUpiResponse(response) } else { onPaymentCancelled() } } fun startUpiPayment(uri: Uri) { val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri) upiLauncher.launch(intent) } Understanding the UPI Response UPI apps return a response as a key-value string . Get Vaibhav Shakya | Mr Neo ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Typical format: Status=SUCCESS&txnId=123456&ApprovalRefNo=987654 Important characteristics: Field names may vary slightly across apps Order of parameters is not guaranteed Some fields may be missing Your app must treat this response defensively. Parsing the Response Safely fun parseUpiResponse(response: String?): Map<String, String> { if (response.isNullOrBlank()) return emptyMap() return response.split("&") .mapNotNull { part -> val keyValue = part.split("=", limit = 2) if (keyValue.size == 2) { keyValue[0].trim() to keyValue[1].trim() } else null } .toMap() } Validating Whether the Response Is Received and Usable A UPI response should be considered received and valid only if: The response string is not null or blank A Status field is present The status value is recognizable ( SUCCESS , FAILURE , sometimes PENDING ) At least one transaction identifier is present ( txnId , ApprovalRefNo , or txnRef ) If these conditions are not met, the response should be treated as cancelled or invalid . Validation Logic fun isValidUpiResponse(response: String?): Boolean { val data = parseUpiResponse(response) val status = data["Status"]?.uppercase() val hasValidStatus = status == "SUCCESS" || status == "FAILURE" || status == "PENDING" val hasTxnReference = data.containsKey("txnId") || data.containsKey("ApprovalRefNo") || data.containsKey("txnRef") return hasValidStatus && hasTxnReference } This check ensures your app reacts only to meaningful responses , not incomplete or interrupted flows. Handling the Final Payment State fun handleUpiResponse(response: String?) { if (!isValidUpiResponse(response)) { onPaymentCancelledOrInvalid() return } val data = parseUpiResponse(response) when (data["Status"]?.uppercase()) { "SUCCESS" -> onPaymentSuccess(data) "FAILURE" -> onPaymentFailure(data) else -> onPaymentPending(data) } } Handling Edge Cases Gracefully UPI flows are external and user-driven. Common scenarios include: User pressing back inside the UPI app App switch or interruption Network delay after debit Missing or malformed response Recommended UX approach: Show a neutral “Processing” state on return Resolve UI state after parsing response Avoid assuming instant success or failure QR-Based UPI Initiation (Optional) UPI QR flows are simply UPI URIs encoded into QR codes . fun generateQrBitmap(content: String, size: Int): Bitmap { val bitMatrix = QRCodeWriter().encode( content, BarcodeFormat.QR_CODE, size, size ) return Bitmap.createBitmap(size, size, Bitmap.Config.RGB_565).apply { for (x in 0 until size) { for (y in 0 until size) { setPixel(x, y, if (bitMatrix[x, y]) Color.BLACK else Color.WHITE) } } } } Any UPI-enabled app can scan and process this QR. Testing Recommendations Always test: Multiple UPI apps Success, failure, and cancellation flows Invalid or zero amount cases App backgrounding during payment Orientation changes Real devices are strongly recommended over emulators. Summary A reliable UPI payment flow on Android depends on: Correct URI construction Modern intent handling APIs Defensive response parsing Explicit validation of recei

content: Beyond Semantics: How to Test Internal Compose State with snapshotFlow Richa Sharma 4 min read · May 1, 2026 -- Listen Share snapshotFlow is a bridge that transforms Jetpack Compose state into a cold Kotlin Flow, allowing you to reactively stream state changes into the world of asynchronous coroutines. Press enter or click to view image in full size credits : unsplash Introduction Imagine you’re building a complex list where a “ Back to Top ” button only appears after the user scrolls past the 10th item. Or perhaps you need to trigger an analytics event only when a certain state combination is reached. In your UI tests, checking for a specific Text label is easy, but waiting for an internal LazyListState to reach a precise offset can feel like trying to catch smoke with your bare hands. This is where many developers get stuck using Thread.sleep() or messy polling loops both of which lead to the dreaded "flaky test." Fortunately, Jetpack Compose provides a elegant, reactive bridge between the world of State and the world of Asynchronous Streams : snapshotFlow . In this article, we’re going to dive into how snapshotFlow works, why it’s the "inverse" of the common collectAsState pattern, and most importantly how you can use it as a secret weapon to write rock-solid UI tests for state that standard Semantics just can’t reach. Understanding the Mechanism Before we use it to fix our tests, we need to understand what snapshotFlow actually does. At its core, it is a bridge. If collectAsState is the door that lets a Flow enter the Compose world, snapshotFlow is the exit that allows Compose State to escape into the world of Coroutines . How it Works snapshotFlow observes any Compose State objects read inside its block. Whenever one of those states changes, the block is re-executed. If the result of that block is different from the last emission (using a standard !=(equals) check), the Flow emits that new value. Example : Let’s look at a common production use case: tracking a scroll position to show a button. val listState = rememberLazyListState() LaunchedEffect(listState) { snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex } .distinctUntilChanged() // Only emit when the index actually changes .filter { it > 5 }      // Only care if we've scrolled past 5 items .collect { index -> println("User is at index: $index") } } Recomposition should be for UI rendering. Logic, API calls, and heavy data processing belong in the Coroutine world . snapshotFlow gives you a thread-safe, reactive way to move that data out of the UI loop and into a background stream. In a standard UI test, you use composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("Submit").performClick() . This works because the "Submit" button is part of the Semantics Tree . Get Richa Sharma ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in However, many things aren’t in the Semantics Tree: The exact scroll offset of a LazyColumn . The internal state of a Pager . A custom Animatable value. If your test needs to wait for the scroll to reach a certain point before clicking a button, you can’t use a standard matcher. The Race Condition Problem Imagine you have a test where you trigger a scroll and then immediately try to click a “Jump to Bottom” button that only appears when the scroll is active. If the test runner checks for the button before the scroll state has updated, the test fails. Solution: Bridging State to the Test Thread We can use snapshotFlow to wait for a specific condition in the internal state before the test proceeds. @Test fun testStickyHeaderAppearsOnScroll() { val scrollState = ScrollState(0) composeTestRule.setContent { MyComplexScreen(scrollState) } // 1. Trigger an action scrollState.scrollTo(500) // 2. Use snapshotFlow to "spy" on the state composeTestRule.waitUntil(timeoutMillis = 2_000) { var isConditionMet = false runBlocking { // We exit the flow as soon as the condition is true snapshotFlow { scrollState.value } .first { offset -> offset >= 500 } isConditionMet = true } isConditionMet } // 3. Now assert with confidence composeTestRule.onNodeWithTag("StickyHeader").assertIsDisplayed() } Why this is better than Thread.sleep() : Speed: It proceeds the millisecond the condition is met, rather than waiting for a fixed duration. Reliability: It hooks directly into the Snapshot system . If Compose knows the state changed, your test knows. No Flakiness: You aren’t guessing how long a transition takes; you are observing the data. If the state is already reflected in the Semantics Tree (e.g., a button becomes enabled), tell the reader to stick to standard Matchers like assertIsEnabled() . snapshotFlow is specifically for when the Semantics Tree is "blind" to the state you need. “When to Use” Comparison Table Press enter or click to view image in full size Summary While snapshotFlow is often tucked away in the 'Side Effects' documentation, it is truly the bridge that connects the reactive world of Compose to the imperative world of testing. By mastering it, you move from testing what the user sees to testing 'h ow the application behaves leading to a more robust and professional codebase. How are you handling complex synchronization in your Compose tests? Have you been stuck using Thread.sleep() , or have you found another way to spy on internal state? Let’s discuss in the comments! Happy coding 💻✨ Until then, if you learned something new today that helped you understand in detail, please drop a few claps to support my writing!👏 Take Care :)

title: Hardening Android Apps: Secure Request Signing with EC Keys
excerpt: Part 5 of the KNewsApp series — where I document the architecture decisions behind a modular, security-first Android news app. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Hardening Android Apps: Secure Request Signing with EC Keys Khizar Khan 6 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Part 5 of the KNewsApp series — where I document the architecture decisions behind a modular, security-first Android news app. In earlier posts I covered the 8-module architecture, Firebase Auth + Credential Manager, and Room v3 auto-migrations. This post is about the :security module — specifically, how KNewsApp signs every authenticated network request with a hardware-backed EC key, and the abstraction that keeps that logic unit-testable. The problem A bearer token alone tells the backend who is asking. It doesn’t tell it what device is asking, or whether the request has been tampered with or replayed in transit. For a news app this is lower-stakes than, say, a banking app, but the pattern is the same one I’ve used in fintech work, and it’s a good excuse to build it properly: sign each request with a private key that never leaves the device’s secure hardware. Step 1: Generating the EC key pair KeyManager lives in the :security module and generates a secp256r1 -family EC key pair directly inside the AndroidKeyStore the first time it's constructed: @Singleton class KeyManager @Inject constructor() : SecurityManager { companion object { private const val KEY_ALIAS = "KNewsApp_EC_Key" private const val ANDROID_KEYSTORE = "AndroidKeyStore" } init { generateEcKeyIfNeeded() } private fun generateEcKeyIfNeeded() { try { val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance(ANDROID_KEYSTORE).apply { load(null) } if (!keyStore.containsAlias(KEY_ALIAS)) { val keyPairGenerator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance( KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_EC, ANDROID_KEYSTORE, ) val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder( KEY_ALIAS, KeyProperties.PURPOSE_SIGN or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_VERIFY, ) .setDigests(KeyProperties.DIGEST_SHA256) .setUserAuthenticationRequired(false) .build() keyPairGenerator.initialize(spec) keyPairGenerator.generateKeyPair() } } catch (e: Exception) { // Log or handle appropriately for production } } A couple of choices worth calling out: containsAlias check before generating — key generation is idempotent across process death and app restarts. The alias, KNewsApp_EC_Key , is only ever created once per install. setUserAuthenticationRequired(false) — this key authenticates the device , not the user. It signs background refresh calls too, so a biometric prompt on every request would be the wrong UX. SHA256withECDSA at sign time — KeyManager doesn't hold onto the key pair; it re-fetches the key from the keystore on every call, which keeps it stateless and safe to use as a Hilt singleton: override fun signData(data: String): String { return try { val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance(ANDROID_KEYSTORE).apply { load(null) } val privateKey = keyStore.getKey(KEY_ALIAS, null) as java.security.PrivateKey val signature = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withECDSA") signature.initSign(privateKey) signature.update(data.toByteArray()) Base64.encodeToString(signature.sign(), Base64.NO_WRAP) } catch (e: Exception) { "" } } override fun getPublicKey(): String { return try { val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance(ANDROID_KEYSTORE).apply { load(null) } val certificate = keyStore.getCertificate(KEY_ALIAS) ?: return "" val publicKey = certificate.publicKey as ECPublicKey Base64.encodeToString(publicKey.encoded, Base64.NO_WRAP) } catch (e: Exception) { "" } } } getPublicKey() matters because the backend needs the device's public key at least once to verify signatures — KNewsApp sends it as a header on signed requests rather than requiring a separate device-registration round trip. Step 2: Signing requests in AuthInterceptor The :network module's AuthInterceptor pulls the session token and, if present, signs the request URL plus a timestamp: class AuthInterceptor @Inject constructor( private val sessionManager: SessionManager, private val securityManager: SecurityManager, ) : Interceptor { override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response { val originalRequest = chain.request() // Get JWT from SessionManager (running blocking for simplicity in Interceptor) val token = runBlocking { sessionManager.userEmail.first() } // For now using userEmail as proxy for token val requestBuilder = originalRequest.newBuilder() if (token != null) { requestBuilder.addHeader("Authorization", "Bearer $token") // Secure Request Signing with EC Keys val timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis().toString() val challenge = originalRequest.url.toString() + timestamp val signature = securityManager.signData(challenge) requestBuilder.addHeader("X-KNews-Signature", signature) requestBuilder.addHeader("X-KNews-Timestamp", timestamp) requestBuilder.addHeader("X-KNews-PublicKey", securityManager.getPublicKey()) } return chain.proceed(requestBuilder.build()) } } The challenge is deliberately simple — URL plus timestamp — rather than a canonicalized request body. The backend can reject a request whose timestamp is stale, which is enough replay protection for this app without the fragility of trying to keep a JSON canonicalization scheme in sync between client and server. Note the AuthInterceptor constructor only knows about SecurityManager , the interface — never KeyManager , and never AndroidKeyStore . That's the seam that makes the next part possible. The challenge: KeyStore doesn’t exist on the JVM KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") needs a real Android device or emulator — the provider simply isn't registered on a plain JVM unit test. content: Android Kotlin Room Database Sqlite Mobile App Development Room Database in Android: From Your First Entity to Production-Ready Offline Storage Ashutosh Kumar 13 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share A practical Kotlin guide covering entities, DAOs, Flow, relations, migrations, testing, and offline-first patterns — with the mistakes that wipe production databases. Press enter or click to view image in full size Room Database in Android: From Your First Entity to Production-Ready Offline Storage TL;DR Room is the Jetpack library that turns SQLite into type-safe Kotlin APIs. Start with Entity → DAO → Database. Observe with Flow , write with suspend . Grow into indexes, relations, transactions, and type converters. In production: export schemas, ship real migrations, never wipe user data on upgrade, and treat Room as the single source of truth for offline UI. Room Database in Android: From Your First Entity to Production-Ready Offline Storage Your users open the app on a subway with no signal. Your product still needs to feel instant. That is the real job of a local database on Android — not “caching for fun,” but durable, queryable state the UI can trust. Room sits on top of SQLite and gives you compile-time SQL checks, Kotlin coroutines, and Flow that re-emits when tables change. This guide takes you from a first Note table to the production habits that keep you from deleting someone’s data on the next release. All samples are Kotlin, self-contained, and ready to adapt. Who this is for Beginners who have never written a Room @Entity Intermediate Android engineers wiring repositories and offline UX Anyone about to ship schema changes and nervous about migrations You will leave with a working mental model, copy-paste building blocks, and a production checklist. Part 1 — Beginner: your first working Room stack What Room is (and isn’t) Room is a persistence library on top of SQLite. You declare tables as data classes, queries as annotated interfaces, and Room generates the implementation at compile time. Room is not a remote backend, a sync engine, or a replacement for thinking about schema versions. If you change a column and bump the version without a migration, Room will refuse to open the database (or wipe it, if you asked it to — more on that later). Why it matters: SQLite is battle-tested. Room makes it less error-prone for Kotlin apps. Dependencies (Gradle + KSP) Use KSP (not the old kapt path) with current Room (2.7.x works well with modern AGP/Kotlin). In your version catalog (or build.gradle.kts ): // libs.versions.toml (sketch) room = "2.7.2" ksp = "2.3.6" // match your Kotlin version // module build.gradle.kts plugins { id("com.google.devtools.ksp") } dependencies { implementation("androidx.room:room-runtime:2.7.2") implementation("androidx.room:room-ktx:2.7.2") ksp("androidx.room:room-compiler:2.7.2") // later: // implementation("androidx.room:room-paging:2.7.2") // testImplementation("androidx.room:room-testing:2.7.2") } Point schema export at a folder you will commit: ksp { arg("room.schemaLocation", "$projectDir/schemas") arg("room.incremental", "true") } The three building blocks @Entity A row in a table @Dao How you read/write that table @Database Groups entities + DAOs + version We will build a tiny Notes app. Entity: define the table @Entity(tableName = "notes") data class NoteEntity( @PrimaryKey val id: String, val title: String, val body: String, val updatedAt: Long, val pinned: Boolean = false, ) Tips for beginners Prefer explicit tableName — refactoring a class name should not rename a production table by accident. Use String UUIDs or server IDs as keys when you sync; autoGenerate = true Int keys are fine for pure local data. Nullability in Kotlin becomes NULL / NOT NULL in SQLite. Be deliberate. Mistake: Putting UI-only fields (like isSelectedInList ) on the entity. Keep the entity a persistence model. DAO: talk to the table @Dao interface NoteDao { @Query("SELECT * FROM notes ORDER BY updatedAt DESC") fun observeAll(): Flow<List<NoteEntity>> @Query("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = :id LIMIT 1") fun observeById(id: String): Flow<NoteEntity?> @Query("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = :id LIMIT 1") suspend fun getById(id: String): NoteEntity? @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE) suspend fun upsert(note: NoteEntity) @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE) suspend fun upsertAll(notes: List<NoteEntity>) @Update suspend fun update(note: NoteEntity) @Query("DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = :id") suspend fun deleteById(id: String) @Query("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE title LIKE '%' || :query || '%' ORDER BY updatedAt DESC") fun search(query: String): Flow<List<NoteEntity>> } suspend vs Flow Use suspend for one-shot reads/writes (sync workers, one-off checks). Use Flow when the UI should update whenever the table changes. Room’s invalidation tracker re-runs the query for you. Mistake: Calling blocking DAO methods on the main thread. With room-ktx , prefer suspend / Flow and never enable allowMainThreadQueries() in release. Database class @Database( entities = [NoteEntity::class], version = 1, exportSchema = true, ) abstract class NotesDatabase : RoomDatabase() { abstract fun noteDao(): NoteDao companion object { const val NAME = "notes.db" } } exportSchema = true writes JSON snapshots under your schemas/ folder. Commit them. Future you (and code review) will thank you. Build a singleton database object NotesDatabaseProvider { @Volatile private var instance: NotesDatabase? = null fun get(context: Context): NotesDatabase { return instance ?: synchronized(this) { instance ?: Room.databaseBuilder( context.applicationContext, NotesDatabase::class.java, NotesDatabase.NAME, ).build().also { instance = it } } } } In a real app you will inject this with Hilt (Part 3). The idea is the same: one open database per process for that file name. excerpt: A few weeks ago, I wanted to solve a problem that sounded almost too easy to be worth a blog post: Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android Development Kotlin Multiplatform Deep Linking Android App Development Kotlin Android App Links: From https://xyz.com/word/hello to Your Android App Rajen Trivedi 9 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share A few weeks ago, I wanted to solve a problem that sounded almost too easy to be worth a blog post: Press enter or click to view image in full size Deep Linking Done Right When a user opens https://xyz.com/word/hello on Android, I want the app to open directly to the hello word. The URL already existed. The website was already live. The Android app was already working. So I assumed this would be a small Android configuration change. It wasn’t. The actual implementation is not especially complicated, but there are several pieces involved, and they all have to agree with each other. Once I understood how those pieces fit together, the setup became much easier to reason about. This article walks through that process from the ground up: what Android App Links actually are, why assetlinks.json is required, where the Play App Signing SHA-256 comes from, how Nginx fits into the picture, how this works in a Kotlin Multiplatform project, and how to verify that everything is working. 1. Start with the Problem, Not the Configuration Before writing any XML or Nginx rules, it helps to define what we actually want. Imagine a website with URLs like: https://xyz.com/word/hello https://xyz.com/word/world https://xyz.com/word/computer When the app is not installed, these should behave like normal website URLs. When the app is installed, I want Android to recognize that the app can handle those links and open the corresponding screen. Conceptually: User taps a URL ↓ Android recognizes the domain ↓ Android verifies the website ↔ app association ↓ The app opens ↓ The app reads the URL ↓ The app navigates to the requested content That last part — reading the URL and navigating inside the app — is only one part of the problem. The more interesting question is how Android knows that xyz.com actually trusts this application. 2. Android Needs Proof That the Website and App Belong Together This is the part that made the whole feature click for me. An Android app can declare that it wants to handle a URL, but that declaration alone does not prove ownership of the domain. Android App Links solve this by creating a relationship between two things: Android app                         Website -----------                         ------- AndroidManifest.xml    <------>     assetlinks.json The Android side says: “I can handle links from this website.” The website side says: “I trust this Android application to handle my links.” Android can then verify that both declarations match. That website-side declaration is the Digital Asset Links file: https://xyz.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json Once I understood this two-sided model, the rest of the configuration felt much more logical. 3. Get the Correct SHA-256 Certificate This is probably the easiest step to get wrong. The assetlinks.json file needs the SHA-256 certificate fingerprint of the Android application that is being trusted. For an app distributed through Google Play, the production application is signed through Google Play App Signing . That means the certificate we care about for the Play-distributed application is the app signing certificate , not simply the upload certificate. In Play Console, you can find the certificate under the Play App Signing section: Google Play Console → Protected with Play → Play Store protection → Manage Play app signing → App signing key → App signing key certificate → SHA-256 certificate fingerprint Copy the SHA-256 fingerprint from there. It will look something like: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF:... One detail worth remembering: if you intentionally support multiple signing certificates, assetlinks.json can contain multiple SHA-256 fingerprints. But every fingerprint you add should represent a certificate you actually need to trust. 4. Create assetlinks.json Now we can create the website-side association. A minimal example looks like this: [ { "relation": [ "delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls" ], "target": { "namespace": "android_app", "package_name": "com.example.app", "sha256_cert_fingerprints": [ "YOUR_PLAY_APP_SIGNING_SHA256" ] } } ] There are only a few values here, but each one is important. relation This tells Android what relationship is being delegated. For normal App Links, the commonly used relation is: "delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls" package_name This must exactly match your Android application ID. For example: com.example.app If the package name is wrong, Android cannot associate the file with your application. sha256_cert_fingerprints This contains the SHA-256 certificate fingerprint of the application that the website trusts. For a Play-distributed production app, use the appropriate Play App Signing certificate. 5. Put the File in the Right Place The filename and location are not optional. Android expects: https://xyz.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json If your website is served from: /var/www/website then the file should physically exist at: /var/www/website/.well-known/assetlinks.json On a Linux server, you can create the directory with: sudo mkdir -p /var/www/website/.well-known Then create the file: sudo nano /var/www/website/.well-known/assetlinks.json At this point, the file exists on the server. content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Object Declarations, Companion Objects & Singleton in Kotlin: A Complete Guide Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share If you’ve come from Java, you’ve probably used the static keyword countless times—for utility methods, constants, or creating singleton objects. But when you start learning Kotlin, one of the first surprises is that there is no static keyword . Press enter or click to view image in full size So how does Kotlin achieve the same functionality? The answer lies in three powerful language features: Object Declaration Companion Object Singleton Pattern These features allow you to create single instances, define class-level members, and write cleaner, more object-oriented code without relying on static . In this article, we’ll explore each concept in detail, understand the differences between them, and see how they’re used in real Android applications. Why Doesn’t Kotlin Have static ? Java uses static members because they belong to the class rather than an object. Example in Java: class MathUtil { static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } } Called like: MathUtil.add(5, 10); Kotlin takes a more object-oriented approach. Instead of static members, Kotlin encourages using objects , ensuring everything belongs to an object rather than existing independently. What Is an Object Declaration? An object declaration creates a class and its only instance at the same time. Unlike a normal class, you never instantiate it yourself. Example: object Logger { fun log(message: String) { println(message) } } Usage: Logger.log("Application Started") Notice that we never write: Logger() The object already exists. Characteristics of Object Declarations An object declaration: Creates exactly one instance. Is initialized lazily (created when first accessed). Cannot have constructors. Can contain properties and functions. Is thread-safe by default. This makes it ideal for shared resources. Singleton Pattern A Singleton ensures that only one instance of a class exists during the application’s lifetime. Before Kotlin, implementing a singleton required extra code. Java example: public class Database { private static final Database INSTANCE = new Database(); private Database() {} public static Database getInstance() { return INSTANCE; } } In Kotlin, it’s much simpler. object Database { fun connect() { println("Connected") } } Usage: Database.connect() That’s all you need. The object keyword automatically implements the Singleton pattern. Real-World Singleton Example Imagine an analytics manager. object AnalyticsManager { fun trackEvent(event: String) { println("Tracking: $event") } } Usage: AnalyticsManager.trackEvent("Login Success") AnalyticsManager.trackEvent("Order Placed") The same instance is shared across the entire application. Object Declarations with Properties Objects can also store shared data. object AppConfig { const val APP_NAME = "ShopApp" var version = "1.0" } Usage: println(AppConfig.APP_NAME) println(AppConfig.version) Since only one instance exists, updates are visible everywhere. What Is a Companion Object? Sometimes you need functionality that’s associated with a class rather than a specific object. This is where companion objects come in. class User { companion object { fun createGuestUser(): User { return User() } } } Usage: val guest = User.createGuestUser() You don’t create a companion object manually. Kotlin automatically creates one for the class. Why Use Companion Objects? A companion object allows you to define: Factory methods Constants Utility functions Shared configuration without creating an instance of the class. Think of it as Kotlin’s replacement for many uses of Java’s static . Companion Object with Constants class ApiConfig { companion object { const val BASE_URL = "https://api.example.com" } } Usage: println(ApiConfig.BASE_URL) This is a common pattern in Android applications. Named Companion Objects A companion object can have a name. class MathUtils { companion object Calculator { fun add( a: Int, b: Int ) = a + b } } Usage: println(MathUtils.add(10, 20)) Although the companion object is named Calculator , you still access its members through the class. Factory Methods Companion objects are frequently used to create objects. class User private constructor( val name: String ) { companion object { fun guest(): User { return User("Guest") } } } Usage: val user = User.guest() This pattern provides controlled object creation. Companion Object Implements Interfaces Unlike Java’s static , a companion object is a real object. It can implement interfaces. interface Factory<T> { fun create(): T } class Product { companion object : Factory<Product> { override fun create() = Product() } } Usage: val product = Product.create() This demonstrates one of Kotlin’s major advantages over traditional static methods. Object Expression (Anonymous Objects) Kotlin also supports creating unnamed objects. val listener = object { fun click() { println("Clicked") } } Usage: listener.click() Object expressions are commonly used for event listeners and callbacks. Object Declaration vs Companion Object Press enter or click to view image in full size Object Declaration vs Singleton Many developers ask: Are they different? The answer is: An object declaration is Kotlin’s built-in implementation of the Singleton pattern. Example: object CacheManager This object is automatically: Singleton Thread-safe Lazily initialized No additional code is required. content: Android Architecture Is Quietly Moving Beyond ViewModel as a State Holder chanzmao 5 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Compose didn’t replace ViewModel. Navigation 3 didn’t replace it either. Together, they’re redefining where state belongs. Press enter or click to view image in full size Image created by AI For years, Android developers followed one simple rule: Put your screen state into a ViewModel. It wasn’t just common advice, it became one of the foundations of Android architecture. TextField values Selected tabs Dialog visibility Scroll position Navigation arguments Business logic Eventually, ViewModels became responsible for almost everything. ViewModel ├── UI State ├── Navigation State ├── Business Logic ├── Repository Coordination └── Coroutine Scope That architecture solved real problems. ViewModel survived configuration changes. SavedStateHandle restored state after process death. Activities and Fragments became much smaller. For the View system, it was the right solution. But Android architecture has quietly evolved. Not by removing ViewModel. By giving every kind of state a more appropriate owner. Compose Changed the Question One of the biggest architectural changes introduced by Compose wasn’t a new API. It was a new question. Instead of asking: Where should I put this state? Compose encourages us to ask: Who naturally owns this state? The official guidance says: You should keep state closest to where it is consumed. That single sentence represents a major shift. For years, developers often moved every UI value into a ViewModel. Compose says something different. Keep state where it naturally belongs. Only move it higher when another layer actually needs to own it. Not Every State Needs a ViewModel Compose makes this obvious with remember . var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") } When the value should survive Activity recreation, Compose provides rememberSaveable . var query by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") } Search queries Selected tabs Expanded cards Dialog visibility Scroll position These are UI concerns. They’re not business logic. Keeping them inside the UI improves locality because the state lives exactly where it’s used. Google No Longer Treats ViewModel as the Only State Holder This architectural shift also appears in the official guidance. Instead of describing ViewModel as the universal place for UI state, Android now introduces the broader concept of state holders . The documentation explains: You can implement a state holder either through a ViewModel or a plain class. That’s an important distinction. A ViewModel is one implementation of a state holder. It is no longer the definition of one. The guide also separates state holders into two categories: Business logic state holders UI logic state holders That separation reflects a much more precise ownership model. ViewModel Is a Business Logic State Holder The official architecture guide explicitly describes ViewModel as a business logic state holder. Get chanzmao ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Its responsibilities include: coordinating repositories preparing data for presentation exposing UI state surviving Activity recreation integrating with Navigation Notice what’s missing. TextField values Dialog visibility Selected tabs Those are UI element state. The documentation even notes that reusable UI components should generally use plain UI state holders instead of ViewModels. Navigation 3 Completes the Separation Navigation 3 continues exactly the same direction. Navigation arguments belong to NavKey . data class UserDetail( val userId: Long ) : NavKey UI state can belong to the destination itself through rememberSeriarizable . var query by rememberSerializable { mutableStateOf("") } Instead of asking ViewModel to remember everything, every navigation entry owns the state that belongs to that entry. Responsibility becomes much clearer. UI State ↓ remember rememberSaveable rememberSerializable Navigation State ↓ NavKey Presentation Logic ↓ ViewModel Persistent Data ↓ Repository Navigation 3 doesn’t replace ViewModel. It removes one more responsibility that never naturally belonged there. ViewModel Is Becoming a State Producer Consider a typical ViewModel. val uiState = combine( usersRepository.users, settingsRepository.settings ) { users, settings -> HomeUiState( users = users, darkMode = settings.darkMode ) }.stateIn(…) Where is the source of truth? Not inside the ViewModel. The repositories already own the data. The ViewModel transforms those streams into something the UI can display. Rather than being a container of mutable state, the ViewModel increasingly becomes a producer of UI state. That’s a subtle shift — but an important one. The Architecture Becomes Simpler The official architecture guide summarizes the idea with a simple recommendation: Hold state as low as possible while maintaining proper ownership. That sentence captures the direction of modern Android architecture. Composable └── UI State Navigation └── Navigation State ViewModel └── Presentation Logic Repository └── Persistent Data Each layer owns the state it understands best. Nothing overlaps. Nothing exists simply because “that’s where we’ve always put it.” What About Configuration Changes and Process Death? Moving UI state out of ViewModel doesn’t mean giving up resilience. Quite the opposite. When every layer uses the mechanism designed for its lifetime, your application can still survive both configuration changes and process death. UI State ├── rememberSaveable └── rememberSerializable Navigation └── NavKey Persistent Data └── Repository The goal isn’t to eliminate state persistence. The goal is to stop using ViewModel as the default owner of every kind of state. Conclusion Compose didn’t make ViewModel obsolete. Navigation 3 doesn’t replace it either. Instead, both libraries are gradually separating responsibilities. UI state

title: Visibility Modifiers in Kotlin: Mastering Access Control
excerpt: Imagine you’re building a banking application. Some functions should be available to everyone, while others — such as password validation… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Visibility Modifiers in Kotlin: Mastering Access Control Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building a banking application. Some functions should be available to everyone, while others — such as password validation or balance updates — must remain hidden from the outside world. If every property and function were publicly accessible, anyone could accidentally modify critical data, making your application difficult to maintain and potentially insecure. Press enter or click to view image in full size This is where Visibility Modifiers come in. Visibility modifiers control who can access classes, properties, functions, constructors, and objects . They help you hide implementation details, expose only what’s necessary, and write safer, more maintainable code. In this article, you’ll learn all four visibility modifiers in Kotlin, understand where each one applies, and see how they’re used in real Android applications. What Are Visibility Modifiers? A visibility modifier defines the accessibility of a declaration. In Kotlin, they can be applied to: Classes Functions Properties Constructors Objects Interfaces The four visibility modifiers are: public private protected internal Each provides a different level of access. Why Do We Need Visibility Modifiers? Suppose you have a BankAccount class. class BankAccount { var balance = 10000 } Now anyone can write: val account = BankAccount() account.balance = -50000 Clearly, this shouldn’t be allowed. Instead, hide the property. class BankAccount { private var balance = 10000 } Now only the class itself can modify the balance. This concept is called Encapsulation , one of the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming. 1. public public is the default visibility modifier in Kotlin. If you don’t specify a visibility modifier, Kotlin automatically makes the declaration public . Example: class User { fun login() { println("Login Successful") } } Usage: val user = User() user.login() Everything is accessible because public is the default. 2. private private restricts access to the declaration within the same scope . For a class member, it is accessible only inside that class. Example: class BankAccount { private var balance = 5000 fun deposit(amount: Int) { balance += amount } fun showBalance() { println(balance) } } Usage: val account = BankAccount() account.deposit(1000) account.showBalance() // account.balance ❌ Compilation Error The balance property is hidden from the outside world. Private Functions Helper functions that shouldn’t be called externally are often marked as private . class LoginManager { fun login() { validatePassword() println("Logged In") } private fun validatePassword() { println("Password Valid") } } Only login() can call validatePassword() . File-Level private In Kotlin, top-level declarations are allowed. private const val API_KEY = "12345" Now API_KEY is accessible only within the same Kotlin file . This is useful for helper functions and constants that don’t need to be exposed elsewhere. 3. protected protected allows access: Inside the same class. Inside subclasses. But not from outside the class hierarchy. Example: open class Animal { protected fun sleep() { println("Sleeping") } } Subclass: class Dog : Animal() { fun rest() { sleep() } } Usage: val dog = Dog() dog.rest() // dog.sleep() ❌ Compilation Error The subclass can access sleep() , but external code cannot. 4. internal internal makes a declaration visible within the same module . A module could be: An Android app A library A Gradle module Example: internal class ApiClient Any file inside the same module can use it. However, another module cannot access it. This is especially useful when creating reusable libraries. Visibility Summary Press enter or click to view image in full size Constructors and Visibility Constructors can also have visibility modifiers. class User private constructor() Now external code cannot create a User directly. Instead, object creation can be controlled using a companion object. class User private constructor() { companion object { fun create() = User() } } Usage: val user = User.create() This is commonly used in factory patterns. Real-World Android Examples Repository class UserRepository { private val apiService = ApiService() } The UI doesn’t need direct access to apiService . Only the repository should interact with it. Singleton object SessionManager { private var token = "" fun saveToken(value: String) { token = value } } The token remains hidden while controlled methods manage access. Base Activity open class BaseActivity { protected fun showLoading() { println("Loading...") } } Every child activity can call showLoading() , but external classes cannot. Internal Library API internal class CacheManager Only classes inside the same module can use it, preventing unnecessary exposure to library consumers. Common Mistakes Making Everything Public Bad: class User { var password = "" } Anyone can modify the password. Better: class User { private var password = "" } Expose only safe operations through public methods. Using protected Without Inheritance protected is useful only when inheritance is involved. If a member doesn’t need to be accessed by subclasses, prefer private . Exposing Internal Implementation Keep helper methods hidden. Bad: fun validatePassword() {} Better: private fun validatePassword() {} Only expose methods that are part of the class’s public API. Best Practices When using visibility modifiers: Keep properties as private as possible. Expose behavior instead of exposing mutable state. Use protected only when subclasses need access. Use internal for module-specific APIs. Prefer the most restrictive visibility that still satisfies your requirements. Hide helper functions and implementation details. Following these principles improves encapsulation and makes your code easier to maintain. Interview Tip A common interview questio

title: Google Play Console Finally Added a Delete App Feature (And Developers Will Love It)
excerpt: For years, there was one thing in Google Play Console that frustrated almost every Android developer. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android Google Play Android Development Mobile Development Kotlin Google Play Console Finally Added a Delete App Feature (And Developers Will Love It) AmitGuptaAppschance 3 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share For years, there was one thing in Google Play Console that frustrated almost every Android developer. You could publish an app , update it , unpublish it , and even transfer ownership — but you couldn’t actually delete it . If you’ve been developing Android apps for several years, your Play Console probably looks familiar: Old hackathon projects Prototype applications Internal testing apps Experimental builds Apps you abandoned years ago No matter what, they stayed there forever. Press enter or click to view image in full size The Old Way: Unpublish Previously, the only option was Unpublish . While this removed the app from the Google Play Store for new users, it didn’t really clean up your Play Console. Here’s what happened: ❌ The app remained visible forever. ❌ Your dashboard became increasingly cluttered. ❌ Test projects mixed with production apps. ❌ There was no way to permanently remove unused apps. For developers who build dozens — or even hundreds — of applications, this became frustrating over time. The New Delete App Option Google has quietly introduced something many developers have requested for years: Delete App This option is available only for eligible apps , but it’s a welcome improvement. Instead of simply hiding an app, you can now permanently remove it from Google Play. Unpublish vs Delete App Feature Unpublish Delete AppVisible on Google Play❌ No❌ NoExisting users can continue using it✅ Yes✅ YesCan receive updates✅ Yes❌ NoCan republish later✅ Yes❌ No (after permanent deletion)Removes Play Console clutter❌ No✅ YesPermanently removes app❌ No✅ Yes What Happens When You Delete an App? When you choose Delete App , Google provides a few important warnings. The app is permanently removed from Google Play. Play Console statistics and historical metrics are no longer available. Existing users can continue using the installed version. Users cannot install the app on new devices. There is a 7-day recovery period before deletion becomes permanent. That recovery window is especially useful in case you delete an app accidentally. Why This Matters At first glance, this seems like a tiny update. But for developers, it’s surprisingly valuable. Many of us have Play Console accounts that are several years old. Over time we accumulate: MVPs Client demos Learning projects Internship assignments Experimental apps Closed testing builds Eventually, the dashboard becomes difficult to navigate. Being able to permanently remove projects makes the Play Console cleaner and easier to manage. Should You Delete Every Old App? Not necessarily. Before deleting an app, consider whether you’ll ever need: historical install data, crash reports, user statistics, Play Store listing information, or analytics. If those insights still matter, Unpublish may be the better choice. If the project is truly abandoned and has no future value, Delete App is finally the cleanup tool developers have been waiting for. Press enter or click to view image in full size Final Thoughts Google Play Console doesn’t often receive features that dramatically improve daily workflows. This isn’t a flashy AI feature or a major redesign. Instead, it’s one of those small improvements that saves developers from years of accumulated clutter. Sometimes the simplest features end up making the biggest difference. If you’ve been waiting for a way to finally clean up your Play Console, now’s your chance. Have you already noticed the new Delete App option? I’d love to hear how many old apps you’re finally planning to remove. content: Android Android Modularization Android Modularization That Holds Up: 5 Lessons for Large Codebases Eury Pérez Beltré 12 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share A practical way to evaluate module boundaries, dependency direction, build conventions, and the rules that keep an Android architecture understandable as it grows. Press enter or click to view image in full size AI-generated editorial illustration. Welcome to this article! 👋 My goal is to help you evaluate Android modularization beyond module count and folder names. We are going to focus on one practical question: do your boundaries actually reduce the cost of change as the codebase grows? What we’ll cover Designing modules around change boundaries. Giving dependencies a predictable direction. Crossing feature boundaries through small contracts. Using convention plugins to make the intended architecture easier to follow. Turning architecture rules into automated feedback. Let’s start with the deceptively easy part. Creating a Gradle module is easy. Give it a name, add a build file, move some code, and update settings.gradle.kts . Repeat that process enough times and you have a multi-module project. The module-count dashboard looks fantastic. 🏆 Everyone can go home. You don’t necessarily have a modular architecture. Sometimes it is just a monolith with excellent folder etiquette. 📁 A project can contain dozens of neatly named modules and still behave like a monolith. A change in one feature may require touching the app module, a shared module, navigation code, and three unrelated features. Every new module may also copy the same SDK versions, Compose configuration, Hilt setup, and test dependencies. The folder tree looks organized. The cost of change tells a different story. Keep one deliberately ordinary change in mind: the catalog needs to open product detail. That path touches two feature boundaries, root navigation, and the build conventions behind both modules. In a weak graph, this small change is enough to expose hidden coupling. This is why module count is a poor measure of modularization. A more useful question is: How much unrelated knowledge does a developer need to make one safe change? The fewer unrelated parts you need to understand, modify, and verify, the stronger your boundaries are. Getting there requires more than moving files. It requires clear responsibilities, predictable dependency direction, narrow contracts, build conventions, and feedback when a rule is broken. With that question in mind, let’s work through the five lessons. 1. Design around change boundaries, not folder aesthetics The first question to ask about a module is not, “What layer does this code belong to?” It is, “Why should this code change together?” That shift matters because a package can organize code without isolating it. A Gradle module creates a stronger boundary. It controls visibility, dependencies, build work, tests, and often ownership. That power comes with overhead, so the boundary should protect something meaningful. The official Android modularization guide makes this tradeoff explicit. Modules that are too coarse can recreate a monolith. Modules that are too fine-grained add build complexity and boilerplate until the structure becomes harder to maintain than the code it was meant to organize. There is no ideal number of modules. There is only a level of granularity that fits the size, rate of change, and ownership model of a project. And no, creating :core:everything does not technically settle the debate. 😅 A useful starting taxonomy might look like this: :app owns the application entry point and final composition. It changes for app identity, root navigation, variants, and final wiring. :feature:* owns a user-facing capability or flow. It changes with the product behavior of that feature. :core:data:* owns data access for one domain. It changes with backend contracts, persistence, mapping, and caching. :core:ui owns the shared design system. It changes with the visual language and reusable UI primitives. :core:navigation or feature API modules own navigation contracts. They change when route or key contracts shared across boundaries evolve. :core:testing owns shared test infrastructure. It changes with test libraries, fakes, fixtures, and helpers. This is a reference model, not Android law. A small app may be better served by :app , one data module, and a few feature modules. A larger checkout domain may justify separate modules for payment, shipping, addresses, and confirmation. The same caution applies to core . A shared module should not become the place where code goes when nobody wants to decide who owns it. If unrelated capabilities change for unrelated reasons, putting them together creates a new monolith with a friendlier name. Eventually, core becomes a junk drawer with a Gradle file. 🗄️ One practical rule is to start local and promote deliberately. A use case needed by one feature can live with that feature. When a second independent consumer appears, you have evidence that the responsibility may deserve a shared contract or module. This is usually safer than predicting every future reuse on day one. A module earns its overhead when it isolates meaningful change without making the codebase harder to navigate. 2. Give dependencies a direction and composition a home Once module responsibilities are clear, the next question is whether a developer can predict the allowed dependencies without opening every build file. A module graph needs a direction. One possible rule set is: :app -> :feature:* -> :core:domain -> :core:data:* -> :core:ui -> :core:navigation :core:domain -> :core:data:* -> :core:models The exact layers can change. The useful property is that dependencies move toward smaller, more stable capabilities and do not casually point back to product features. This is also why :app deserves a specific job.
