title: Offline Sync Conflicts on Android: Keep Pending Edits Safe and Choose a Policy You Can Explain
excerpt: Part 3 of the Room / offline-first series — version numbers, last-write-wins, field merges, 409 Conflict, and UI that does not silently… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Jetpack Compose Database Room Database Mobile App Development Offline Sync Conflicts on Android: Keep Pending Edits Safe and Choose a Policy You Can Explain Ashutosh Kumar 9 min read · 1 hour ago -- Listen Share Part 3 of the Room / offline-first series — version numbers, last-write-wins, field merges, 409 Conflict, and UI that does not silently trash the user’s words. TL;DR Conflicts are normal once two devices edit offline. Pick a policy you can explain to product: usually server-wins for pull , but never overwrite local rows that still have pending outbox work . Use a monotonic version (or updatedAt with care), optionally merge non-overlapping fields, surface true conflicts in the UI, and test the matrix: pending vs not, remote newer vs older, push 409. In Part 1 Room became the single source of truth. In Part 2 an outbox + WorkManager pushed offline edits and migrations stopped wiping history. This part answers the question every offline app eventually hits: Phone A and Phone B both changed the same note. Who wins — and what happens to the loser’s words? You do not need a PhD in CRDTs to ship. You need a policy , a few lines of code that enforce it, and tests for the ugly cases. What a “conflict” actually is A conflict is not “the network failed.” A conflict is: two writers produced divergent versions of the same entity , and a simple overwrite would drop someone’s intent. Classic timeline: t0  Server note v1: "Buy milk" t1  Phone A offline → "Buy milk and eggs"   (local v2, PENDING) t2  Phone B online  → "Buy oat milk"        (server now v2) t3  Phone A comes online → push or pull? If Phone A’s pull blindly applies server v2, A loses “and eggs.” If Phone A’s push blindly overwrites the server, B loses “oat milk.” Neither bug is Room’s fault. Room stored both truths faithfully. Sync policy decides which truth survives. Principles before policies Pending local work is sacred. If an outbox row still exists for an entity, do not clobber that Room row with a pull. You would delete the user’s unsent edit from the UI. Policy must be product-visible. “Server wins” is fine if users expect shared docs to reconcile to the cloud. “Client wins” is fine for a personal scratchpad. Silent mystery merges are not fine. Versions are cheaper than regret. A monotonic version: Long (or server-assigned revision) beats guessing from wall-clock updatedAt alone. Detect, then decide. HTTP 409 Conflict on push is a gift — handle it; do not retry forever pretending nothing happened. Add version to the note (recap) @Entity(tableName = "notes") data class NoteEntity( @PrimaryKey val id: String, val title: String, val body: String, val updatedAt: Long, val version: Long = 0, val deletedAt: Long? = null, val syncStatus: SyncStatus = SyncStatus.SYNCED, val pinned: Boolean = false, ) On every local edit: val pending = note.copy( body = newBody, version = note.version + 1, updatedAt = System.currentTimeMillis(), syncStatus = SyncStatus.PENDING, ) The server should also own a version. Ideal flow: Client sends version it based the edit on (or the new version it proposes — pick one API style and stick to it). Server rejects stale writes with 409 when the base version is behind. Mistake: Using only updatedAt from the device clock. Clocks skew. Two devices can both look “newer.” Prefer server versions when you can; treat device timestamps as UX metadata. The decision function you will reuse Here is a small, testable policy used by many offline apps (including server-wins pull that refuses to smash pending work): object ConflictResolver { /** * Should a pull overwrite the local Room row with remote data? * * - If local has pending outbox work → never accept remote for that entity. * - Otherwise accept remote when remoteVersion >= localVersion (server-wins / LWW by version). */ fun shouldAcceptRemote( localVersion: Long, remoteVersion: Long, hasPendingLocalChanges: Boolean, ): Boolean { if (hasPendingLocalChanges) return false return remoteVersion >= localVersion } fun <T> resolveServerWins(local: T, remote: T): T = remote fun <T> resolveClientWins(local: T, remote: T): T = local } Unit tests — keep these forever: @Test fun acceptRemote_whenNoPendingAndRemoteNewer() { assertTrue( ConflictResolver.shouldAcceptRemote( localVersion = 1, remoteVersion = 2, hasPendingLocalChanges = false, ), ) } @Test fun rejectRemote_whenPending_evenIfRemoteMuchNewer() { assertFalse( ConflictResolver.shouldAcceptRemote( localVersion = 1, remoteVersion = 99, hasPendingLocalChanges = true, ), ) } @Test fun rejectRemote_whenRemoteOlder() { assertFalse( ConflictResolver.shouldAcceptRemote( localVersion = 5, remoteVersion = 4, hasPendingLocalChanges = false, ), ) } Why hasPendingLocalChanges wins over version math: The pending row is the user’s latest intent that has not reached the server. Applying remote now creates a false “SYNCED” UI and orphans or confuses the outbox payload. Wire it into pull / refresh suspend fun applyRemoteNote(remote: NoteDto) { val local = noteDao.getById(remote.id) val pending = outboxDao.hasPending("notes", remote.id) val accept = local == null || ConflictResolver.shouldAcceptRemote( localVersion = local.version, remoteVersion = remote.version, hasPendingLocalChanges = pending, ) if (accept) { noteDao.upsert(remote.toEntity(syncStatus = SyncStatus.SYNCED)) } // else: keep local PENDING/FAILED row; outbox still owns the next push } ASCII: Pull remote note │ ├─ no local row ──────────────────► upsert SYNCED │ ├─ local has outbox pending ──────► keep local (skip remote) │ ├─ remote.version >= local.version ► upsert SYNCED (server-wins) │ └─ remote older ──────────────────► keep local Policy menu (pick one per product surface) 1) Server-wins (default for shared data) Meaning: Cloud is authoritative once local pending is cleared. title: I rebuilt my flashlight app five years later
excerpt: In 2021 I shipped an Android flashlight app. Then I forgot about it. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android Mobile App Development Flashlight Jetpack Compose Indie App I rebuilt my flashlight app five years later Teemy 5 min read · 4 hours ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Blinker — Auto Flash Light In 2021 I shipped an Android flashlight app. Then I forgot about it. Last year I opened Play Console and found it removed . The reason had nothing to do with the code: a missing Data safety form — a declaration Google introduced in 2022 — and the warning emails had piled up in an inbox I no longer read. Opening the project to revive it went worse. There was no source. All that survived was the AAB sitting in Play Console. So I built it again from nothing. That is what I am shipping today. Blinker App Link : https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.teemy.autoflashlight Why a flashlight app in 2026 Honestly: if all you want is on and off, you don’t need one. Android already has a torch tile in Quick Settings, and it is faster than any app. This one does something else. It uses the torch as a signal . Riding a bike at night, telling the car behind you that you are there A car stopped on the road, warning whoever is coming round the bend A blacked-out building, telling someone two floors up where you are A crowd, on the beat None of those are about “ON”. They are about **how it blinks** . Press enter or click to view image in full size Blinker App Main Screen You can record your own rhythm This is my favourite part. In REC mode, hold the pad and the light is on; let go and it’s off. That gets recorded. Whatever rhythm your finger taps out becomes a flashlight pattern. Afterwards you can **trim it like a video clip.** Drag the white handles to pick the part worth keeping, and only that part is saved. The fumble at the start, the silence at the end — cut them off. You also choose whether it plays once or loops until you stop it. Press enter or click to view image in full size Blinker REC Record and trim editor Up to 60 seconds. Somebody is going to tap out Morse and save it, and I want to see that. What comes built in The slider goes from 0.1 to 60 flashes per second . That said, most phone LEDs cannot actually hit 60Hz — the real rate is whatever the hardware manages. The app says so on screen rather than pretending otherwise. Presets reorder by long-pressing and dragging , and anything you don’t use can be deleted. Press enter or click to view image in full size Blinker App Presets Without opening the app When you need it, hunting for an app icon is already too late. Home screen widget — one tap, straight into whatever pattern you used last Quick Settings tile — pull down the shade, done Both can be added from inside the app (Settings → Shortcuts). Press enter or click to view image in full size Blinker App — Home screen widget About safety A strong strobe can trigger photosensitive seizures. Including in people with no history of them. So there is a safety notice on first launch, and an on-screen warning whenever you enter the danger band — 3 to 30 flashes per second. The notice is not skippable. That may read as heavy-handed for a flashlight, but a bright light blinking fifteen times a second is genuinely a hazard. The app also never asks for camera permission. It drives the flash LED and does not capture anything. If a flashlight app asks you for camera access, it is fair to wonder why. For anyone opening it the first time Instead of a feature tour, there’s a tutorial you actually do. Across fifteen steps, one part of the screen stays lit and the rest dims. Nothing except the highlighted control responds, so there is no way to wander off mid-step. You turn the torch on yourself, record a pattern yourself, and save it. At the end it offers to add the widget and the tile for you. Skippable at any point, and repeatable later from Settings. Sixteen languages English, Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Russian, Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, Arabic, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Filipino, Amharic. Arabic and Urdu mirror the entire layout right-to-left. On a fresh install it follows your system language, and you can change it in Settings whenever. On building it A full rewrite. Jetpack Compose, Material 3, targetSdk 36, Android 7.0 and up. Exactly two things carried over from the old app: the package name and the signing key. Those two are why existing users get this as an update rather than a stranger. Not one line of the code survived. What took longest was not features. It was the small stuff. Dragging a preset kept catching. The cause was not the animation — reordering was cancelling the drag gesture outright, every time The tutorial spotlight wobbled because it was chasing the scroll. Moving it into content coordinates instead of screen coordinates fixed it The recording waveform only moved when you let go. Now yellow grows while you hold and grey grows while you don’t, live None of that earns a line in a feature list. I think you feel it anyway. Get it [Blinker on Google Play] [ Teemy Youtube ] Android 7.0+. Free. If something’s off or missing, tell me. I’m especially curious how the LED behaves on hardware that isn’t my Galaxy — the ceiling on blink rate varies a lot between phones.

Productivity Android Technology Self Improvement Mindfulness 5 Android Settings Quietly Draining Your Focus (Not Just Your Battery) Amal Amin 2 min read · 8 hours ago -- Listen Share I used to blame my phone for feeling scattered. Notifications kept pulling my eyes back to the screen, and I’d lose the thread of whatever I was actually trying to do — write, read, just think. I assumed that was just what phones do now. Then I went through my settings one evening, mostly out of boredom, and found a handful of things quietly working against my attention the whole time. None of them were dramatic. All of them added up. Here’s what I found, and what I changed: 1. Adaptive notifications were " helpfully " reordering my alerts. Android tries to guess which notifications matter most and bumps them to the top — which sounds useful until it starts training you to check your phone more, not less. Turning this off made notifications boringly chronological again, which somehow made them easier to ignore. 2. Every app had permission to send " priority " alerts. I never remembered granting this to half of them. A shopping app treating a discount code like an emergency is not a priority alert. I went through and stripped this down to the handful of apps that actually deserve it — messages, calls, calendar. 3. Always-on display was showing more than the time. Mine was quietly surfacing message previews every time I glanced at my phone for the clock. I wasn’t opening the app, but I was reading it — which is its own kind of interruption. Switched it to show just the time and date. 4. App timers existed, but I’d never set any. I always assumed "digital wellbeing" tools were more gimmick than help. Setting a soft limit on the two apps I mindlessly opened most — not blocking them, just a gentle nudge — cut my pickups more than I expected. 5. Auto-brightness was tuned for visibility, not comfort. This one’s less about focus directly, but a screen that’s slightly too bright makes everything feel more urgent than it is. Dialing it back made scrolling feel less compulsive, oddly enough. What This Actually Changes None of these changes took more than a few minutes combined. What surprised me wasn’t that they existed — it’s that they were all defaults I never chose, just settings that came pre-decided for me. If your phone has been feeling louder than it should, it’s worth checking whether you actually picked these settings, or whether they picked themselves.
